speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days
ago the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) made a request that, when the estimates for the Department of National Defence were presented for consideration by the committee of supply, there might be a statement made by the responsible minister, in the first place with reference to the general principles of the defence policy, and in the second place with reference to the question of general administration.
I would therefore ask the indulgence of the committee if in response to that request I might be permitted, as briefly as possible, in the first place to review the general funda-

Supply-National Defence
mental principles underlying the present defence policy of the Dominion of Canada; in the second place to review the purposes for which the votes given last year were expended, and in the third place to make an analysis of the estimates for 1938-39. May . I say at once that I regret that the hon. gentleman who made the request is prevented through an indisposition from being here this afternoon. He will, however, be granted every facility in the way of general discussion on a future occasion.
In reviewing the evolution of the defence policy of Canada it might be important to examine, not for any authoritative purposes but purely from the historical point of view, some of the declarations made at former imperial conferences. We might review also the declarations of policy which were made in this House of Commons in 1936 and 1937 and refer briefly to some of the findings of the imperial conference of 1937 in connection with national defence.
It might be worth recalling that a resolution was passed in 1923, reaffirmed by the conference of 1926, which ended with this important declaration:
The primary responsibility of each portion of the empire is for its own local defence.
The conference of 1926 was responsible for the famous Balfour formula with reference to Canadian status. In connection with the matter of foreign relations, which is closely connected with the question of national defence, may I quote the resolution passed in 1926:
It was frankly recognized that in this sphere, as in the sphere of defence, the major share of responsibility rests now and must for some time rest with His Majesty's government in Great Britain. Nevertheless all the dominions engaged to some extent, and some to considerable extent, in the conduct of foreign relations, particularly those with foreign countries on their borders. . . . The governing consideration underlying all discussions of this problem must be that neither Great Britain nor the dominions could be committed to the acceptance of active obligations except with the definite assent of their own governments.
In historical retrospect I think I can safely deduce that the following principles emerged from these imperial conferences:
First, that each self-governing portion of the empire is primarily responsible for its own local defence. Second, that the security of the empire is a matter of concern to all its governments. Third, that military action taken at any time, in peace or war, is a matter for individual decision on the part of each empire government.
It might be interesting to recall the resolution passed by the chiefs of staff of the subcommittee on imperial defence in 1923-I quote:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom is mainly responsible for the security of the communications between the several parts, of the commonwealth.
And also:
Each of the several dominions is responsible-for protecting its territory and coastal trade against aggression until support comes from the outside.
Between 1926 and 1936 there was no pronouncement of major importance with reference to the question of national defence. May I just emphasize the fact that the pronouncements made by the imperial conferences of 1923 and 1926, after the promulgation of the Balfour formula in 1926, are practically synonymous with the pronouncements made under the new Canadian status acquired since 1926; in other words, the aspects of national defence and the defence of Canada have been emphasized. Speaking in this house on February 12, 1936, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had this to say:
While declarations on behalf of Canada on the subject of the defence of Canada have been made at various imperial conferences, as may be seen from the results thereof published from time to time, I am not aware of any commitments made on behalf of Canada with regard to imperial defence. At such conferences it has been expressly recognized that it is for the parliament of the several parts of the British commonwealth of nations, upon the-recommendation of their respective governments, to decide upon their course.
Then on March 10, 1936, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I should add that we have made clear at various conferences that any action in the-nature of military obligations of any sort would be entered into by the government of the day only after such had been recommended to parliament by the government and approved by parliament itself.
May I be permitted to refer again to the debate that took place in this house on February 19, 1937, when the general principles with reference to our defence policies were laid down very carefully by the Prime Minister. I do not intend to refer in detail to the remarks he made at that time, but I should! like to put the following on the record:
When some of us to protect ourselves and our country against the forces of blood and of death ask parliament to vote money for purposes of defence, that we may continue to further the law of peace and work and health we are told that we are preparing for and promoting war. We are doing nothing of the kind. We are trying to make the national
Supply-National Defence

position secure to enable the law of peace, work and health to prevail and progress. This we believe is only possible as we keep at bay those forces that are making for death and destruction.
And again:
By all means, let us make the most of our friendship with the United States. _ By all means, let us make the most of our friendship and kinship with Great Britain and with every other part of the British empire. By all means let us continue to be friends with every other nation, because in that direction, more perhaps than in any other, security lies. But let us realize that unless we do something to help ourselves these countries cannot be expected to help at a time of world crisis, or great peril. It is not contended that that danger is great for us. There is a danger but so far as Canada is concerned, it is, as I have already pointed out, an incidental contingency. Relatively our danger is small. Another great war, however, might lead to exposure to dangers, which might be great indeed.
May I be permitted to quote shortly from what I said on February 15, 1937:
National security, national defence, the *direct defence of Canada, of our coastal areas, *our ports, our shipping terminals, our territorial waters, the focal areas of our trade routes adjacent to our harbour mouths-these *are the matters dealt with in these_ estimates. May I tell my hon. friend there is no new defence policy embodied in these estimates. There is no new policy here at all. These estimates represent only an honest attempt by those who for the time being are charged with responsibility for the national wellbeing, to see to it that we have something effective and efficient for the purposes of direct defence of Canada or for defending our neutrality should it be assailed by anyone outside.
During the course of that discussion there [DOT]was in progress throughout Canada a comprehensive review from various angles of thought of the necessities of the defence policy. May I be permitted to submit to the committee this afternoon, without either comment or criticism, the various expressions of opinion that were in evidence throughout Canada during the debate in the house last year. I think it is safe to say that there were five schools of thought at that time in the dominion.
In the first place, there was what might be called the imperialistic school, which regarded Canada as an integral part of the British commonwealth, bound to support every other member of the commonwealth with military action and bound to accept the foreign policy of the United Kingdom government, Whether that policy was arrived at independently or through consultation. The slogan of that school probably was: When Britain is at war Canada is at war and is bound to throw her whole weight into the conflict.

The second school of thought was the isolationist or nationalist or North American, which held that Canada's geographical position and economic interest required that she dissociate herself from responsibility for troubles in other parts of the world, especially Great Britain's European complications and her imperial commitments in Africa, the far east, et cetera. In wars arising from such situations, according to this school, Canada would not participate.
The third group, in my judgment, at that time consisted of league collectivists, who would have Canada participate in international obligations for peace. Some of these would go so far as to have Canada participate in military sanctions. Others would not, especially if the hostilities were remote from Canada.
The fourth group, a very minor group, were the North American collectivists, who would have Canada join the Pan-American Union as a league of nations for the western hemisphere and unite with all other American nations in taking only so much interest in European and Asiatic affairs as might be consistent with purely American interests.
The fifth and I think largest group might be termed the moderate or the middle group, believing in no automatic commitments either for military action or for neutrality. These would join with Great Britain or with the league in war for a principle or for the safety of the liberty of the world if convinced that that liberty was seriously threatened. But they refuse to imperil Canadian unity by accepting in advance either one of the two following propositions: first, that when Great Britain is at war Canada must automatically go to her support with all her resources; or secondly, that when the league orders sanctions, Canada is bound to take action.
This I think is by far the largest group of Canadian public opinion; it was last year and I believe is this year, and the formula is that parliament, representing the public opinion and the public sentiments of the Dominion of Canada, must decide on every occasion as these issues arise. With reference to that sentiment the following declaration was made:
In practice this will not mean a rigid policy expressing itself in automatic action or inaction as trouble arises, but a policy in keeping with conditions and circumstances. In so far as we come to parliament with an expression of our opinion we will give it to parliament from the point of view that a certain course should be taken because, having regard to all the circumstances existing at the time, we believe it to be in Canada's interests it should be taken.

Whose statement is that?

Supply-National Defence

That is the Prime Minister of Canada speaking.
Having had the benefit of what was a very evident clarification of the issues surrounding public sentiment regarding the defence policy for Canada both in this house and in journals outside, ministers representing the government of Canada, the Prime Minister and four of his colleagues, were privileged to take part in that great imperial conference of 1937. To conclude the continuity of quotation with reference to the evolution of the present defence policy of Canada, based not upon any historic conference but upon the realization by those responsible for government in this country of the necessities of Canada at the present time, may I put on the record one or two short quotations from the findings of the imperial conference of 1937. But may I be permitted, first of all, to make this declaration, that every single minister who represented Canada at that imperial conference in 1937 was bound regarding declarations made there with reference to national defence or foreign policy, by the declarations made to this parliament during the debates last year, and no pronouncement of any kind was made during those discussions of the imperial conference except along lines similar to the pronouncements made in this house a year ago.
Referring to defence, the official findings of the imperial conference have these words:
The conference gave close attention to the subject of defence, and considered ways in which it would be possible for the governments concerned to cooperate in measures for their own security. The occasion was taken for a detailed review of the state of defence in each of the countries represented at the conference and this opportunity was generally welcomed. . . .
The members of the conference noted with deep concern that since the session of 1930, international tension had increased in a marked degree, and that there had been a large and rapid increase in the armaments of all the principal powers. They were impressed by the world-wide effect of these increased armaments on the international situation and on the financial and economic position of the nations concerned, and while their respective parliaments had already recognized the necessity for taking measures to put their defences in order, they thought it of the highest importance that negotiations for the limitation of armaments should be reopened whenever there was a reasonable prospect of success. They recognized with regret that . . . international conditions were not at the moment favourable to further progress in the direction of disarmament.
And this final quotation from the findings of the imperial conference:
In the course of the discussions, the conference found general agreement among its members that the security of each of their
countries can be increased by cooperation in such matters as the free interchange of information concerning the state of their naval, military and air forces, the continuance of the arrangements already initiated by some of them for concerting the scale of the defences of ports, and measures for cooperation in the defence of communications and other common interests.
Then this vitally important paragraph:
At the same time the conference recognized that it is the sole responsibility of the several parliaments of the British commonwealth to decide the nature and scope of their own defence policy.
This is very important-the conference recognized that it is the sole responsibility of each parliament of the commonwealth to decide the nature and scape of its own defence policy. That is all I intend to say, Mr. Chairman, with reference to the historical continuity of the evolution of what is to-day the defence policy of Canada.
Now I come very briefly to review the activities consequent upon the expenditures authorized by parliament in 1937. The main estimates voted last year were, roughly speaking, $36,000,000. The purposes for which these were asked were described in parliament in great detail in the debate to which I have alluded. May I say immediately that substantial progress has been achieved through the year in carrying out the program which was then described. Additional equipment, supplies, structures and premises have been acquired, and part of the increased vote went for pay and allowances and maintenance of an increased personnel in the naval and air services. Increased training for the militia was also provided.
Speaking directly of the naval service, there was last year for pay and allowances an increase of $358,000. partly accounted for by the pay and allowances of an increased complement of 13 officers and 360 ratings, as the new destroyers that were purchased last year from Great Britain required a greater complement than the old destroyers, which were demilitarized. The personnel also of the new mine-sweeeprs now under construction had to be trained. The net increase in the complement of the naval services was 345, including ten officers. The complement of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve was increased from 875 ratings to 1,017 ratings.
In regard to stores and allowances, amongst the items acquired were naval guns and mountings; torpedoes; ammunition for guns, including service and practice outfits; antisubmarine defences for Esquimalt and Halifax; mine-sweeping outfits, and anti-submar* ine equipment of various kinds for ships.
Supply-National Defence

Four new mine-sweepers are now under construction, and they can be discussed in detail when we come to the items that concern them.
With reference to the militia services item, there was an increase of $3,372,000. The chief purposes of these increases were as follows: to provide better training for the nonpermanent militia; to provide for preliminary work on new coast defence fortifications, chiefly on the Pacific coast; to add to the supply of ammunition and technical equipment, and for the construction of new buildings and works required for the activities of the several services.
Coming to the non-permanent active militia, there was an increase there of $220,000, nine-tenths of which was applied to improving the training efficiency of the non-permanent forces. To give details: Fortress and antiaircraft troops were given nine days' extra training; infantry troops were given two days' extra training, and the minimum of five days in camp for all cavalry and infantry units was reintroduced after some years. This meant an increased cost of $132,000. Other increases were occasioned by the tactical training of officers, the numbers attending the militia staff courses, and qualifying courses for personnel of units converted by reorganization.
Coming to the permanent force increase of $168,000, an increase of about three per cent, this is accounted for in part by increase in personnel of 22 officers and 173 other ranks. This was somewhat offset because 9 officers and 80 other ranks who were on the strength of the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals were previously included in the estimates for civil aviation and are now transferred to the Department of National Defence. That brings me up to the estimates now before the committee, the estimates for 1938-39. Let me say at once that the purpose of these estimates is to continue work that was commenced last year, and within the same definite limitations announced to this house a year ago: in the first place, for the preservation of Canadian neutrality; in the second place for the defence of our Canadian coast line, the defence of our ports and terminals, and the defence of the focal areas of our trade routes in case of necessity. A certain amount of priority has been established after deliberation: first for the air services; secondly,

for naval defence; and thirdly, in regard to the repairing of deficiencies in equipment of militia services, permanent and non-permanent. to undertake an investigation of the possibility of establishing a fishermen's reserve on the Pacific coast; and once that is done it will be followed by the establishment of a similar reserve on the Atlantic. Substantial additions will also be made to the reserves of service ammunition for the air force during the year. The new magazine in the interior of British Columbia will be completed and a magazine near the Atlantic coast will be provided.

Let me now say just one word with reference to the functions of the air force in connection with the government's program. A well equipped and efficient air force is, in my opinion, of primary importance for the protection of Canadian territory and waters, and in view of the rapidly increasing performance of modern aircraft the possibility of attack by such means is to-day a probability. Apart from its value as a highly mobile striking force capable of rapid concentration at any point in Canada, it is alsq required to assist the other services in their particular role of defence: in the first place, independent air action against enemy aircraft and bases, and air action in conjunction with ground antiaircraft defences of important localities; in the second place cooperation with naval forces in the protection of trade routes and focal points of shipping; and thirdly, cooperation with the militia by observation of coast artillery fire and assistance in the suppression of enemy landings and raids.
With reference to the militia services, in the present estimates there is a reduction of $2,733,216, accounted for by the fact that deliveries cannot be made and the amount is regarded as fairly reasonable. In regard to the non-permanent militia, provision is made for an additional day's training and for more camp training instead of training at headquarters. In regard to the permanent militia, provision has been made for increased training and allowances, has also been made for the increased costs of rations and fuel. In regard to fortifications, $1,000,000 has been allotted for the fortifications on the Pacific coast. Last year the amount was $895,000. In regard to general stores, provision is being made for the acquisition of coast defence guns and mountings, fire control equipment and communications; anti-aircraft guns and mountings; machine guns, mortars and anti-tank weapons and field battery headquarters equipment; searchlights, both mobile and fixed; mechanical transports, includings tanks, and ammunition. It is anticipated that delivery cannot be obtained during the coming year of all the equipment which is to be ordered, and the funds provided in these estimates will cover the extent to which deliveries are anticipated during the year.
With reference to militia services there has been carried out by the department what is known as an interim plan of armaments for both coasts. This is a result of the fact that heavy ordnance cannot be acquired from British concerns for a period of about three years. But interim plans have been carefully prepared, in collaboration with an expert adviser, and these estimates are to provide in
part for the completion of these interim plans. As I have said, these plans have priority on the Pacific coast, but eventually they will apply to the Atlantic coast as well. In regard to the survey that was made last year, that has been concluded on both coasts, and a complete plan is available in the department with reference to the defence of both coasts of the Dominion of Canada.
The next consideration, therefore, is this: Having analysed the general principle of defence policy; having explained what was done with the money voted last year; having made a brief review of the estimates for this year, what are the actual problems before a general staff with reference to the defence of Canada? In the first place, what are the possible dangers, and in the second place what are the objectives of the department, in preparing plans to meet them? Some of our critics might say that these estimates are inadequate. Others might say that possibly they will involve commitments. Others might say that any policy of military preparedness is a contribution to the international armaments race. With reference to commitments may I say that none exist. With reference to the adequacy of the estimates may I say that they are carefully prepared to meet the situations supposed to be those with which we might be confronted. In regard to the militaristic point of view, I think every member of this government and every member of this house would be very glad indeed if these moneys did not have to be spent on national defence at this time. But we must meet the conditions in which we live. These are most disturbing times, with the international situation full of tremendous possibilities of danger and disaster, and we owe it to our people, we owe it to our duty towards the security of Canada, to do something reasonable and rational to protect our people and our country.
The purpose of the armed forces of any country I think may be threefold: In the first place, to support peace time diplomacy; in the second place to provide a deterrent to aggressive nations; and in the third place in case of hostilities to be used after the methods of diplomacy have failed. The interests to be defended by arms, if that regrettable necessity should arise in Canada, are first of all the protection of our Canadian territory, and in these estimates, Mr. Chairman, there is not the slightest suggestion of aggression or of menace against any person or any country in the whole world. They are all based upon What is reasonably assumed to be necessary for the defence of our Canadian territory, and

I feel sure that everyone, not only in this House of Commons but throughout Canada, if the need should ever arise is prepared in the ultimate issue to defend the homes and institutions of our people in this dominion. I feel that is a reasonable assumption. Then we have the defence of those institutions of learning, the cultural institutions and the great bequests of justice and freedom which are ours, despite economic strife in this country. As someone has said in regard to the essential requirements of the defence of Canada, patriotism and pacifism are combined in a positive form and a positive faith. The second necessity would toe in regard to our foreign trade. We are an exporting and importing nation. We produce tremendous quantities of food supplies, and in case of an emergency between two belligerents that would bring its own economic consequences. Therefore Canada must be ready to preserve her neutrality and to defend herself against raids from any quarter.
In regard to the exact position of Canada it is only fair to say that to-day the main deterrent against a major attack upon this country by a European power is the existence of the British fleet in north Atlantic waters. An attack on Canada's overseas trade at the most congested points on our coasts in the opinion of those most competent to observe and advise would be limited to minor raiding forces. Just as the British navy on the Atlantic is our greatest security in that quarter so I think it might be reasonable to assume that in a major conflagration we should have friendly fleets upon the Pacific ocean, and the severity of raids upon our western seaboard would be limited toy the strength and the position of these friendly fleets. Our major defensive buffer on the Pacific coast is not the Pacific ocean alone but the existence there of friendly fleets. There is no commitment or understanding in regard to these matters, but at this time I think reasonable assumptions are justifiable.
Now, sir, in regard to the scale of attacks upon Canadian territory or Canadian ports or terminals, these are considered by the experts who are supposed to be qualified to offer advice to be, in the first place, minor attacks by combined sea, land and air forces, to destroy something of strategic or commercial value, or to secure an advanced base of operations, and this applies to coasts, to focal sea areas and to the preservation of Canadian neutrality; in the second place, sporadic hit and run raids by light cruisers or submarines to destroy our main ports and focal sea areas. If that be the situation; if that is a 
correct description of potential dangers, then what are the defensive requirements needed in Canada to meet them? In the first place, for the defence of our focal sea areas we require sea and air forces capable of finding and destroying hostile service craft, submarine or aircraft raiders, and this requires aircraft and naval strength. That is why the small naval force of Canada is being increased by two destroyers at the present time. A slight increase in our naval forces is vital and essential, in cooperation with air and militia services, for the preservation of our neutrality, and the defence of our focal areas, our trade routes, our terminals and our ports. Secondly, for the defence of our main ports we have the anti-aircraft defences, army cooperation aircraft, fighting aircraft and ground troups. For the preservation of our neutrality it is considered that the requirements are a constant patrol of the coastal areas by auxiliary services, aircraft and bombing craft, and troops.
May I, therefore, summarize the situation in regard to defence policy. The task of a defence policy in Canada to-day is, first, to decide on the broad defensive requirements necessary to give effective protection to national interests which if necessary should be protected by force of arms; second, to define the individual and collective functions of each part of the broad defensive organization; third, to decide on the organization, strength, composition, equipment and distribution of the sea, land and air forces as demanded by their individual and collective tasks; fourth, to permit of effective organization, to control, coordinate and provide for not only the activities of the three fighting services in peace and war but of the whole national effort in war, and fifth, to provide the funds necessary to give effect to the requirements, I have just stated.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say this: I have endeavoured to review Canada's defence policy up to the conclusion of the imperial conference of 1937. I have analysed the estimates of 1937-38 and the purposes behind the estimates of 1938-39. I have endeavoured to deal with the actual necessities confronting Canada, and the requirements of defence to meet these potential perils.
When, sir, as we do now, we contemplate the broad principles of Canadian defence, and endeavour to define with some particularity the responsibilities that rest with governments; when, as now, we are confronted with very grave international problems which at any moment may explode against the ordered progress of our national life in the Dominion of Canada; when we realize that the greatest necessity in Canada in regard to defence and

other policies is the unity of our Canadian people; when we realize that no policy having regard either to national defence or to foreign affairs which does violence to Canadian unity is of very great value either to us in Canada or to others outside; when we witness the apparently inevitable divisions of modern nations into the friends of freedom and the friends of force; when the nations of democracy seem to be driven to the defence of their ideals against the nations of the dictators-if the clash is inevitable, and if the clash must come; if the cherished liberties of our civilization are imperilled, then it is that perhaps Canada, seeking to preserve national unity, must look back to the beginnings of her history, must assess the great treasure of culture that came from old France and the institution of ordered government that came from Great Britain; must realize how much the union of the great national legacies meant to the early days of settlement and of government, and also looking to the newer land to the south, consolidated through a valiant insistence upon the tradition of freedom; must be prepared, for the preservation of the best there is in these three nations and the best' there is within her own boundaries-the best there is in democracy itself

to take her stand, if need be, against brute force and might and ruthlessness, and, if need be, for high purposes to endure sore travail.
We are a free people. We are very free, but we are still subject in this Canadian land to old kinships, old sentiments and very old loyalties. We, all of us in this country, love peace. We hate and despise war. Governments with great sincerity proclaim policies and pronounce dogmas, but no matter what the dictates of government may be, the people and the opinion of the people always decide the ultimate issues.
In my judgment, Canada is definitely opposed to extraneous commitments of any kind and to any type of extraneous entanglements. But public opinion in Canada to-day is in favour of a rational policy composed of reasonable measures for the defence of Canada. And public opinion in Canada, the opinion of the people, regardless of the action or inaction of any government, in the final analysis will decide the issues which may arise in the future.
All we can do, then, in this house at the present time, in the consideration of these estimates, is, in the spirit of that old Greek sailor mentioned by Seneca, in the spirit of real unity, to do the best we can:
O Lord; you may sink me, if you will; you may save me, if you will; but at least I will keep my rudder true.

The armament estimates provide the members of the house this year as last, with an opportunity to state their views on the question of national defence. I intend to deal with the subject, as I did on a former occasion, without regard to sentimental or ideological considerations, but in the light of facts and from the sole standpoint of Canada's best interests.
May I begin by briefly recalling the circumstances which attended the voting of the defence appropriations for the last fiscal year?
The consideration of last year's estimates was preceded by an educational campaign which assumed various forms; for weeks and months we were the object of a sustained effort designed to develop in this country an imperialistic sentiment. The London Times went so far as to hint that the dominions would assume part of the cost of British rearmament. The combination of war preparations in Europe and increased military appropriations in Canada afforded some reason for doubt, to say the least, particularly on the eve of an imperial conference.
In view of our geographical position and the international situation, existing at that time, all causes of conflict having apparently disappeared-the conquest of Ethiopia having become an accomplished and accepted fact; Germany having, by scrapping the Treaty of Versailles and reoccupying the Rhine demilitarized zone, satisfied its pride; Japan giving no cause for uneasiness; and the gentleman's agreement concluded between Great Britain and Italy on January 2, 1937, having apparently settled the difficulties which had arisen in connection with Spain and the Mediterranean-I could not see at that time any danger of attack justifying an increase which seemed to me disproportionate to our needs and our means.
I asked for particulars and guarantees, but those I received did not seem to me to be sufficient.
Nevertheless, though refusing my support, I stated my readiness to vote any amount required to ensure the defence of Canada, but in Canada only. I asserted my opposition to any participation in a foreign war and to any preparations for such a purpose.
We were told that the appropriation was solely for the defence of Canada. But when I asked the Minister of National Defence where our first line of defence was, I obtained no definite reply carrying any reassurance, but rather an evasive answer tending to inspire if not fear, at least serious doubt, for the

dispelling of which not a single statement issued from the government before the vote was taken.
Such were the circumstances of my refusal to vote for the increased appropriation. My opposition, mark you well, was based not so much on the expenditure involved as on the fear that it was intended for war outside of Canada.
Has there occurred any change in the situation since then, either in Canada or elsewhere?
In the months of May and June last, there was held in London an imperial conference at which defence was the chief subject of discussion. Despite the appeals of those who wished to involve Canada in a policy of imperial defence, our delegates showed a most commendable attitude.
The Summary of Proceedings states that the Conference recognized that:
it is the sole responsibility of the several parliaments of the British commonwealth to decide the nature and scope of their own defence policy.
and that:
the increased programs of armaments were no more than sufficient for the defence of their (that is, the countries represented) territories and trade and the fulfilment of such obligations as each might have assumed.
Then the Prime Minister, in a speech he delivered on his return from the Conference, spoke as follows:
Canada made no agreement to participate in any _ military campaign undertaken by the empire or the League of Nations.
These definite statements show the truly Canadian attitude adopted by our ministers. They serve, Mr. Chairman, to dispel the apprehensions raised by the increased appropriations of last year.
Here is another important fact. Last October a highly-placed man made the following remark:
Canada is a sovereign nation and a Canadian's first duty is not to the British commonwealth but to Canada.
Then came the Lotbiniere and St. Henry elections.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere reminded the House of the statements made throughout the campaign, in which the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Health took part. He said:
My friends and I stated at every public meeting that we were in favour of defending our country, that we believed that our first line of defence was now in Canada, but that we were against spending one cent to arm or equip an expeditionary force-in short that we did not intend to take part in any foreign war.

The same language was used in St. Henry where the Minister of Public Works and the Secretary of State asserted their opposition to joining in any foreign war and stated that not one cent of the 1937 appropriation had gone into preparations for war outside of Canada.
The Minister of National Defence, called upon for a statement, affirmed that- the estimates contained no appropriation for an expeditionary force, but provided only for the defence of Canada against those who might attack us or violated our neutrality.
And on January 21st last the Minister of Justice said to the delegates of the Federation of National Catholic Unions:
I notice that your brief contains this sentence:	The Federation of National Catholic
Unions is against Canada's participating in any foreign war. Such is also my view of the matter.
Finally, the estimates for the coming fiscal year show a reduction of $4,551,401 in the contested items.
All these facts, Mr. Chairman, tend to set our minds at rest regarding the aims of the government's defence policy.
I now come to the international field. The situation abroad, dominated by the armaments race, is far from reassuring. Fortunately Canada does not appear to be taking part in the race with any hope of winning, as she has diminished her appropriations while other countries have considerably increased theirs.
Let us examine the sequence of events.
Italy which, since the Ethiopian conquest, one would ibe inclined to class among the satisfied nations, is becoming more and more threatening; she asks her people for guns instead of bread.
Germany wants colonies and wants to obtain them by force rather than by compromise. "Less and less butter and more and more guns," was the statement recently made by a minister of the Reich. Germany seeks to extend her influence wherever there are Germans.
Japan, which we thought happy since her conquest of Manchuria, has developed a still greater desire to expand. One wonders where she will stop.
Nations no longer consider themselves bound by treaties. They adhere to them only so long as it serves their interest to do so.
These three great nations do not hesitate to say that they place their reliance on force and antagonism. They have made an agreement known as the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo axis. Though threatened by no one, all three consent to the greatest sacrifices in order madly

to arm themselves by day and by night. For what purpose? Not to defend themselves, for no one thinks of attacking them.
So we see small, peace-minded countries of Europe, like Sweden, Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and others increase their armaments in order to defend their territory, to defend their neutrality.
Let us look further into the matter. What is Italy's present policy? Though no one is disputing her colonial empire, she is increasing her fighting capacity, despite her poverty.
Notwithstanding the gentleman's agreement which she signed with England on January 2, 1937, she continued her intervention in Spain not for the purpose of obtaining foodstuffs to improve the condition of her people, but in order to obtain raw materials needed for war. She has designs on all sides-in Spain, in Africa, in Egypt and elsewhere.
She is maintaining three armies outside of her home territory: one in Ethiopia, one in Lybia and a third in Spain, which are exhausting her resources. With an army, a navy and an air force whose needs are constantly increasing, she is practically devoid of coal and oil.
While claiming that her conquest of Ethiopia was dictated by vital necessity, her actions show that her policy is a policy of aggression and that she cherishes designs of conquest and domination.
The statements uttered by Mussolini at the beginning of the year regarding the laying down of further units do not indicate any slackening in that respect.
Germany's policy is still more alarming. Having torn up the Treaty of Versailles, of which only the territorial clauses and the dispossession of her colonies are left, having freed herself from all the restrictions imposed upon her national sovereignty, having provided herself with a formidable army equipped with modernized artillery, and an air force daily becoming more powerful, she intends reconquering her colonial empire, with the aid of Mussolini, whose visit to Berlin in September last has consolidated the alliance of the Italian and German peoples.
On November 20, 1937, Hitler said:
Within six years, Germany shall have reconquered her colonies.
On December 10, Mr. Goebbels declared:
Naturally, the four-year plan is also intended for war.
On December 12 when Mussolini announced Italy's resignation from the League of Nations he said, with a flourish of his sword:
On land, on sea and in the air, our arms are numerous and sharp.
And Hitler, in his speech of February 20, spoke as follows:
Year after year Germany will insist more and more on the return of its former colonies of which she was deprived by nations who have no use for them, while for us they are indispensable.
The return of the colonies remains one of the articles of the program which Hitler and Mussolini are together seeking to carry out.
Encouraged toy the success of her foreign policy, strengthened by her military revival, Germany has been demanding with ever-increasing insistence the return of her former colonies ever since Mussolini gave Italy's official approval to her claims at a great Fascist demonstration held in Rome last November. And she seeks to justify her colonial claims by economic reasons.
Let us see whether these claims are based on real economic need or simply on considerations of prestige.
In the course of a speech which he delivered in March, 1937, at the International Academy of Diplomacy in Geneva, Mr. Amery, a former Secretary of State for the Colonies and Dominions in the British government, showed with the aid of statistics that
-before the war the German colonies played a negligible part in the Reich economy; all together they accounted for only six-tenths of one per cent (0-6%) of Germany's exports and five-tenths of one per cent (0-5%) of her imports.
The loss of her colonies has obviously not prevented Germany from obtaining the supplies she needed and their restoration would not suffice to alleviate her scarcity of raw materials. In any case, Germany has since the war traded with her former colonies now under mandate on a footing of absolute equality with all the other powers, and she sells to them more than she buys from them.
As for essential raw materials, statistics show that 90 per cent of the world production comes from- independent countries and only 10 per cent from colonies properly so called.
Are the colonies necessary for the settlement of a surplus German population?
The answer is no, for in 1914 there were only 24,000 Germans in all the German colonies, of which only 18,000 were on the African continent. Moreover, if Germany needs space for her surplus population, how is it that she has just concluded with Italy an agreement under which she is to admit 30,000 labourers for farm work in the spring?-
In order to satisfy Germany, it would be necessary to redraw the boundaries of the entire world. And there is reason to believe

that Germany's desire to recover her colonies is based on considerations of strategy or of prestige and pride.
How far will she go in the direction of territorial claims to satisfy her hunger for domination? Hitler's recent speech and the Austrian developments are rather disquieting. The Chancellor, speaking to the whole world, made known his intention to take under his protection the German minorities living in the neighbouring states. We might well ask ourselves, what next? There are now in Germany four to five million men employed in armament plants. And press dispatches report that the conscription has been decreed of all youths leaving school in order to enroll them in production.
Military conscription, economic conscription, everything tends towards war. Every budget contains national defence appropriations. The new improved motor roads were built with strategical uses in mind. From May, 1935, to November, 1937, Germany is said to have expended 8 billions of dollars in armaments and she has not finished. Where will all this lead to? Lucien Romier stated the question as follows in its relation to the Japanese aggression :
Seeing Japan make such profitable use of her armaments, how much longer will Germany, strained to the utmost, and Italy, exhausted by her efforts, restrain themselves from attempting to obtain some benefit from their own armaments ?
The attitude shown by Japan since last summer has injected into the international situation a new element of uneasiness and is most ominous for Canada. This new Japanese invasion of China has once more upset the friends of peace.
A proletarian nation, Japan, according to a French economist, has managed, without having in its islands a single raw material, to attain third place among the industrial empires of the world. Her population is overflowing. Had she not in Manchuria, which she conquered, and in her other possessions a sufficient outlet and source of supply? Nevertheless, without a declaration of war, she launches her forces once more upon China in quest of additional territory. It seems obvious that Japan, either to obtain raw materials for its industries and space for its surplus population or to enhance her imperial prestige, seeks to dominate the Pacific. In any case, at the end of December or the beginning of January a Japanese minister, Admiral Suyetsugu, launched an appeal to the yellow race to free itself from the domination of the white race.
Ever since last summer the Japanese have been bombarding civilian populations and at-

tacking neutral ships. In August last the British ambassador was machine-gunned while travelling from Nanking to Shanghai. Later on the American ship "Panay" was sunk and the British ship "Lady Bird" bombarded.
Whether it is a matter of economics or prestige, it is certain that Japan is pursuing a great war of conquest which not only affects China, but threatens the interests and even the possessions of other nations. The question is how far her ambition extends. Is she aiming at the conquest of the whole world?
In the face of the alarming attitude of these three great warlike nations which have joined forces in the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo axis, the other nations which do not desire war have deemed it wise to undertake themselves rearmament programs of inconceivable proportions. Great Britain's program for this year involves an expenditure of 1,700 millions of dollars. That of France, 1,000 millions of dollars. That of the United States, 1,200 millions. And smaller nations such as Holland, Sweden, Belgium, Switzerland, to name only a few of them, fearing the worst, have increased their armament appropriations to an extent that compels them to practise the most rigid economy in other matters.
The uneasiness felt by every country in Europe has crossed the seas and affected our neighbour the United States. In the early part of the year President Roosevelt proposed an expenditure of more than one billion dollars to strengthen his navy and aviation, specifying that it was not for purposes of aggression but solely for national defence. To Chairman Taylor, of the House of Representatives Appropriations Committee, he said:
Recent international developments have caused me a great deal of uneasiness. . . . It is my duty to maintain a jealous watch over national defence. When I say uneasiness, I have no particular nation in mind. It cannot be denied that many nations of the world are constantly increasing their armaments. I have made every possible effort to stop this disastrous race, but I have not succeeded. Facts cannot be denied. The United States, like all other nations, must recognize them.
Mr. Cordell Hull, Secretary of State of the United States, reaffirmed the ends sought by his country in its defence program. In a letter of February 12 last to Democratic Representative Ludlow, after stating that while guarding from extreme isolation the government wishes to avoid all alliances and entanglements, he said:
If every peaceful nation were to insist on remaining entirely aloof from every other peaceful nation and on pursuing a policy of armament limitation without reference to

relative armaments, the inevitable consequence would be that other nations inclined to play-lawless roles would thereby be given great encouragement and even assistance towards so doing.
And in. connection with the naval rearmament program, he said:
All of the ships and auxiliary services provided for in the proposed program are needed for the national defence of the United States and its possessions. Even with these increases, our navy would not be able to embark upon offensive or aggressive operations.
This new orientation of American policy constitutes in the international field an event of decisive importance for Canada; it determines our own policy.
Glancing at the map and contemplating the immense body of water that separates the American continent from Asia, the possibility of a successful attack appears very remote indeed. But on the other hand, if we take into account the improvement and rapidity of means of attack, if we think of the defence preparations effected in the course of the last few months by the American people, the most peaceful on earth, for the protection of their Pacific coast, which adjoins Canada

an air base at Sitka Harbour, Alaska; another one at Dutch Harbour in the heart of the Aleutian Islands, 1,380 miles from the Japanese air base on the Kuril Islands; improvements to the Hawaii Islands naval base; an aerial station at Tacoma to protect the country against a possible threat from Japan by way of the Aleutian Islands, Alaska and British Columbia-is there not cause for uneasiness on our part?
Such is the history of the past ten months. An armament race accompanied by the pursuit of raw materials. An insatiable hunger for domination. World peace threatened from all sides by the dictatorships. The minds of these people instead of being directed towards peace are more and more directed towards war. The whole world is arming.
According to recent documents from Geneva, the expenditure on armaments in 1937 amounted to 33 million dollars a day, and it will be still greater in 1938.
In the face of such an international situation, where do we stand? Are we exposed to attack or to a violation of our neutrality? Wherein lies the guarantee of our security?
The League of Nations had for a time given hopes of security to peaceful nations. Unfortunately, following a series of successive
failures, she has lost the means of preventing conflicts. I will remind the committee of only a few of these failures, in connection with the great powers whose actions are the cause of the greatest worry for peaceful nations.
In 1931 Japanese aggression against China in Manchuria, in defiance of three basic treaties: the Covenant of the League of Nations, the Washington treaty (also known as the nine power treaty), and the Briand-Kellogg pact.
In 1935 Italian aggression against Ethiopia, violating four treaties: the League Covenant, the three-power convention of 1906, the Briand-Kellogg pact, the Italo-Abyssinian treaty of friendship of 1928.
In 1936 Germany reenters the demilitarized zone of the Rhine, in spite of the Versailles treaty and the Locarno pact.
In each of these three cases the League of Nations bowed before the fait accompli.
As a writer has said: "The fundamental principle on which the league is based, that of collective security, crumbled down when the disheartening fatality that, even to oppose the use of force one must be in a position to use force, was made known to the world."
Is our geographical position a protection in itself? Assuredly, on account of the distance between us and the three bellicose powers, the danger of aggression is rather remote, but not entirely abolished. With modern means of transport, which are constantly being improved, and with the greater speed of aeroplanes and ships, oceans grow narrower, distances grow shorter.
Are not the United States as far away from them as we are? They entertained no apprehension last year. But, see what they are doing now. If they feel the need of protecting themselves on the Pacific, does not the same need exist for us also? In the case of a conflict between Japan and the United States, what would become of our neutrality?
Last year, Mr. Bourassa said, in connection with the military appropriations: "Against whom are we rearming? Against Japan? There might be something in the idea."
Would England or the United States protect us? As far as England is concerned, we cannot expect from her anything that goes beyond her own interest. If we want to be free from any obligation towards her that would involve us in a world war, we cannot demand anything of her. But, even if her interest compels her to defend our country, would it be possible for her to do so in a scattered war? Recent statements in the British House of Commons settle the question.

As for protection, from the United States, it cannot relieve us of the duty of contributing something. And let us bear in mind that protection inspired only by interest is not to be fully relied upon. Italy conquered Ethiopia to the detriment of English interests. Japanese have taken possession of part of China to the prejudice of English and American interests. However, neither England nor the United States have intervened in defence of the countries attacked.
What country could attack or invade Canada?
We cannot think of any possible enemy. But we see countries arming themselves to the teeth, not for defence purposes, because nobody is attacking or threatening them, but with a view to conquer new territories, to strengthen their economic independence and satisfy their appetite for expansion and domination. Their attitude is becoming more and more threatening.
We cannot think of any possible enemy. But our country is endowed with unrivalled and varied resources which arouse the cupidity of those countries hankering after raw materials. The visit of German engineers to Anticosti island, last December, was prompted by the desire either to secure raw materials or to establish a military base, and one is as alarming as the other.
Ethiopia had no enemies, but she had natural resources. China had no enemies, but she was a source of supply and an outlet for the surplus population of Japan.
To-day, countries always find a way of justifying any attack.
Belgium had no enemies in 1914, her neutrality was guaranteed by a treaty. She was nevertheless invaded. Sweden, Holland, Switzerland have no enemies, but they are arming for their own defence. Our neighbours, the United States, have no enemies, but they also are arming, and how!
If we have no enemies, there are at least those who disturb our peace and who give us cause for reflection.
What is Canada's duty?
In this early part of the year 1938, we are faced with three great powers: Germany, Italy and Japan, whose armaments, ambitions and (plans are the more alarming as the international situation grows more strained. Events seem to have conspired against the friends of peace and unarmed security. The moral appeasement that could be expected in the early days of 1937 has not materialized. Facts speak for themselves.
It is impossible for us to maintain an ideological policy; we have to face realities. Our

state of sovereignty involves the duty of providing for our own defence and safeguarding our neutrality. The best way to develop a Canadian sentiment is to be prepared to rely on ourselves rather than on others.
It goes without saying that we must avoid being entangled in any external conflict.
When we see what is going on in Europe, Africa and Asia, where Great Britain has interests to safeguard, we realize how our association with members of the commonwealth might have serious consequences if it involved for us any obligation of taking part in a war in which one member might be engaged.
As an aftermath to the Ethiopian conflict, we are faced with the Egyptian crisis, in which we can see the clash between English and Italian influences.-In Europe, we have a dispute for the control over the Mediterranean, as a consequence of the Spanish war. In the Far East, it is the Japanese thrust in China with all its effects in the economic field.
Assuredly, Great Britain appears to know how to take blows when necessary. Nevertheless, she has interests on the five continents and the cause of conflicts are numerous.
The Statute of Westminster has made Canada a sovereign nation with all the liberties implied by that word; most precious of all being the liberty to avoid getting killed for the protection of the interests of others. At the present time Germany is asking for the return of her former African colonies, which have been divided among all the members of the commonwealth with the exception of Canada. Well, can you imagine. Canada fighting in order to keep those colonies under their control?
Our interests are in America, because Canada is an American country, and our attitude in military matters must not be determined by the attitude of Great Britain, whose interests are so numerous and varied in all parts of the world, but by the attitude of our neighbour, the United States of America, who entertain no warlike views.
Let me read to you a resolution passed some time ago by the Canadian Students' National Congress, as reported by Le Droit of February 11:
Canada owes it to herself to formulate a program of moderate rearmament in order to strengthen her coastal defences. Canada must not be a party to a plan of collective defence for the _ countries of the empire, but must rather aim at a system of tacit cooperation with the United States in that respect.
And the newspaper commented on these resolutions as follows:
The two resolutions taken together are acceptable.

Canada enjoys the great advantage of being in America. Defensive armaments, unimportant in themselves, become powerful in our country against a distant enemy who could attack us only under disadvantageous circumstances due to the great distance, and only at the risk of provoking a friendly nation or a nation interested in our defence.
Like all other peaceful countries, we are compelled by necessity. The defence of our country cannot mean preparing for war; on the contrary, it means striving to avoid it by discouraging in advance those who might have in mind to attack us for any reason whatever.
As Lyautey said:
Showing one's strength is the best way to avoid the necessity of using it.
We cannot advertise to the whole world or let everybody believe that Canada would be an easy and defenceless prey for anybody who would like to attack it or simply invade it. Therefore I am in favour of a defence policy, based on our autonomous condition, on our desire for peace, on our geographical situation, on our financial means, and having for its sole purpose the safeguarding of our neutrality and the protection of Canada, in Canada.
What estimates are we asked to vote for National Defence purposes?
According to the blue book, they amount to $34,034,384. As a matter of fact, military appropriations are not over $32,766,594.
There has been included this year in the estimates for National Defence, under item 180 and items 194 to 198, a total of $911,770, that had never before been included in those appropriations, but were in the estimates for Civil Government, Northwest Territories and Miscellaneous. Item No 193-Civil Aviation, an amount of $356,000, covers expenses in connection with topographical air surveys for the Mines and Resources Department, and is also a non-miltary item. All the above-mentioned items, forming a total of $1,267,770, though administered by the National Defence Department, are not actually military appropriations and must be deducted from the amount of $34,034,364.
I should have liked to make a few observations on the four items about which I and some members differed last year, but time will not allow. It will be sufficient to say that they have been reduced by $4,551,401, compared with the amounts voted last year and that I have satisfied myself, with the aid of the particulars printed in the blue book and the information I have received, that the four items cover, for the greater 51952-105
part, maintenance and renewal expenses. As for the votes in connection with the new undertakings, they will be used to erect buildings that cannot be moved from one place to another, to purchase two destroyers and a number of planes necessary for our Pacific coast defences.
I took the trouble to make a careful study of the defence appropriations. And, if I have decided to support them, it is for the reason that, having made a serious review of the international situation in the light of the developments of the last ten months, I believe them necessary for the defence of our country and the safe-guarding of our neutrality; it is because, following a careful study of the various items, I am satisfied that they will serve exclusively for the defence of Canada, in Canada only.
As I do not believe in systematic distrust any more than in blind confidence, and having regard to the attitude adopted by the right hon. the prime minister in a number of cases, particularly in 1922 on the occasion of the Chanak incident when he refused to embark Canada in a war at the request of Lloyd George-then on the occasion of the Locarno treaty,-at Geneva, in September 1936, and above all at the Imperial conference held in London during the months of May and June last, I have reason to believe that, always animated with truly Canadian sentiments, he never will entangle Canada in a foreign conflict in which she would have no interest to defend; and by so doing he will contribute greatly to maintain unity in our country.

There is a reduction in these estimates of $2,000,000 from last year's total of $36,000,000 odd. This is a large sum of money compared with past votes, but it is necessary, and I am glad that the government has given to the house an opportunity to discuss the great question which at the moment means so much to the people of Canada, as it does to the people throughout the British empire. The defence of the empire is a matter of life and death, because if Britain fails the world will go out into outer darkness and we in common with the rest of the world will lose our liberties and the civilization we enjoy. The Canadian people are very much concerned about the whole question; it is one of the questions uppermost in their hearts and minds to-day-" Whither Canada "? That question is on everyone's lips.
So far as defence is concerned we are back where we were in 1812-complete dependence on the motherland for protection. We have never had any adequate defence policy nor

have we had adequate defence forces to protect our shores. We have been depending upon the mother country for the preservation of our liberties and our civilization. We can talk about this estimate of $34,000,000, but it is a mere drop in the bucket compared to what the people of the motherland have to pay for the defence of the empire. I have a great deal of respect for the Prime Minister; he is a gentleman whom I have known for a great many years, and I am sure that everyone sympathizes with him, for his burden at the present time is a heavy one. Under our constitutional practice, 'however, as the Prime Minister is aware, seeing that he has had a great deal of experience in diplomatic affairs, it is the duty of parliament to inquire into estimates such as those we have before us to-day and to see how the trust reposed in the Prime Minister and the government has been discharged.
I do not agree with the policy of silence in matters of this sort. I remember that before the great war, in 1914, Pield Marshal the late Lord Roberts was laughed at in England and his speeches called pernicious and dangerous because, even up to three days before the outbreak of war, he predicted it. A number of public men in England-Asquith, Haldane, Runciman, and some of the most prominent men in public life there-were of the opinion that there would be no war; they had found a way of preventing it. There had been silence about foreign affairs and the defences of the country. That should be a lesson to us to-day in Canada in considering the question now before us. In my opinion silence is a mistake; it is far better for the government to take parliament and the country into its confidence and to indicate the exact state of affairs.
I am glad to see that the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Raymond), coming as he does from the province of Quebec, realizes the importance of national defence. The people of that province have always been loyal to the mother country and I am glad to see that its representatives are taking the stand that adequate defences and armaments are necessary. During the St. Henry by-election the Minister of Public Works and the Secretary of State, with other younger speakers, took the stand that adequate defences were necessary for this country. But adequate defences of themselves without adequate man power, as has been said very well by a great public man, are inadequate, and I believe the support of adequate defences for Canada is a sound position for the people of Quebec to take because, with British Columbia, it is

among the most exposed provinces of Canada, so it is necessary there for us to have adequate defence.
The second point I wish to advance in regard to these estimates is that every gun and every soldier to man a gun brings us nearer not war but peace, as was said by the minister for war in England the other day. I am glad that stand has 'been taken. Nobody in Canada wants war. The Minister of Pensions and National Health and the Minister of National Defence know what war means, but even those of us who could not or did not go during the last war have seen the awful suffering that resulted on the part of men, women and children throughout the country then and since. Everyone in England and Canada hates war and the very mention of war. The very idea of war is hated and detested by everyone; nevertheless preparation is necessary. You will not hear one word in favour of war either in England or in Canada. It is right to hate war, but we have to face the facts. There is the question of the defence of liberty and civilization. In England they have been slow to get started, but they have recognized the mistake they made in this army, and now they are a unit in rearming. At Norwich the labour unions voted in favour of rearmament by two and a half million to less than two hundred thousand. It has been forced upon England, and these expenditures have been forced upon the government and people of Canada by the situation existing outside this country. The government does not want it; the opposition does not want it. No one wants to spend all this money unless it is necessary, but it is necessary with the conditions that exist in the world to-day, and armaments for Canada are a necessity.
Canada has tried conscientiously to carry out all its various treaties, peace agreements and pacts. They have been carried out to the letter. The Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, the former prime minister, as heads of the government of this country, did their best to carry out our obligations in regard to the League of Nations and peace. They did everything they could in the public interest, but what happened? The League of Nations has had no greater support than has been given by England and Canada. To-day England stands before God as the trustee of the peace of the world. It finds the league in ruins, and is brought to the very verge of war for disarming.
We have been slow to see this coming upon us, and I say to the government of the day that something should be done to take the people of the country into their confidence and let them know what are the real facts.

No longer can officials of our external affairs and defence departments consider these matters as their sole responsibility. That was the situation in England up to 1914, but afterwards they were sorry for it. We should not make a similar mistake now. I only wish to offer constructive suggestions, and I believe the government should now trust the people completely in regard to Canada's foreign policy and Canada's defence policy. We should have all the information now, so that we can tell our constituents in order that the country may know what it is all about. This is not the private affair of our Department of External Affairs or the officials of that department. They should not keep these things secret. Let the government tell parliament plainly the extent of our obligations to Great Britain and the other dominions. We should have a statement of the facts. We should know who are our friends in world politics to-day, and who are not. We should know the differences of opinion that may exist between the. motherland and the south of Ireland and South Africa or between the other dominions and Canada on defence and foreign matters, if there are any differences, as I know there are. We should know the facts with regard to our obligations to these dominions, the British Empire and our friends in Europe.
I say we should not only consult and advise with Great Britain. We will have no time for that if the enemy sail up the St. Lawrence and blow up the citadel, or attack the Pacific coast. Then it will be too late, as it was in 1914. We should know what nations are threatening us, who are our friends, who are our foes; the extent of our own defences and arms on land, sea and in the air; what deficiencies there are in our armed forces, and what is required. This vote is only a drop in the bucket compared to what will be necessary in the future if this policy continues the world over. We should know what is necessary if we are to maintain adequate defences and adequate reinforcements, not only in regard to guns but in regard to munition plants in Canada. All the munitions used in Canada should be manufactured here, so far as possible by those out of employment. In the St. Henry iby-election the Minister of Public Works referred to the venerable cannon and the horse drawn artillery. We should know What guns, munitions, transports, equipment, clothing and rations will be needed, and what merchant marine we have to carry food to England. Our memory is very short, but we saw what happened to Belguim in 1914, when she was unprepared, and there was secrecy and silence respecting her defences until it was too late. Do we want it to happen again?
I am glad to see some advance in the policy with regard to the air force. Since we have been a country we have never had any policy of defence. To-day, as in the war of 1812, we are depending on the mother country. There is a vote of $10,000,000 for the air force, but you know as well as I do that with aeroplanes capable of travelling 250 miles an hour an enemy can leave their base, do damage to municipal institutions, public utilities, government buildings, schools and hospitals, and return very rapidly. So I think we should have a proper air force. During the last great war Canadians led the world as air men. They were the best at the front, and what we did then we can do again.
Then there is the question of national service. I have not heard any reference to this, although I believe the minister has done something about it. There should be some form of voluntary national service here, on educational, social and practical lines, and business men should help. We have a large number of young people out of work, walking the streets and taking the dole. If there were some system of training similar to that proposed by the minister of war in England they could enlist for a five year period, during which they could learn a trade, and get some pay and lodging, clothing and equipment, etc. They would receive physical as well as military training, and many of them could be employed as air mechanics, pilots and workmen. It would be a form of preparedness in regard to man power, which as I have said is just as necessary as adequate defences and adequate armaments. I think it would do a great deal to solve the unemployment problem.
I want to congratulate the Chamberlain family. The great Joseph Chamberlain gave us this dream of imperial preference and imperial federation out here, with a trade policy wrapped up in defence and migration. Great services were performed by his late lamented eldest son, Right Hon. Sir Austen Chamberlain, and the present Prime Minister of England, Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain, whose wise judgment and uncanny way of accomplishing things and steadying affairs in times of stress is a great asset in times like these. The Chamberlain family have always been well disposed towards Canada. Their trade preference policies have done much for this country. I am glad to see that in Great Britain at the present time a man who has kept a steady head is heading the government. If ever England needed a George Canning, she needs him now. We have to-day the same condition of affairs which existed in 1823 after the great Napoleonic war. At that time
