England had a prime minister named George Canning, one of the greatest prime ministers, so far as his dealings in connection with foreign affairs were concerned, that the mother country ever had. He brought peace to Great Britain. For over a hundred years there has not been a civil war in that country.
I congratulate the present Prime Minister of Great Britain upon saving the dominions and the motherland from war. I believe he will go down into history for what he did in the past month. In addition to that, he is a modern George Canning. I believe that if the present government in Great Britain carries * out the commitments it has now in the way of promises and pledges and makes no more, the policy of the motherland will be based upon that of George Canning, of keeping out of European affairs as far as possible and preserving peace-at any rate until Britain is armed.
What is Canada's defence policy? Whither is Canada going in foreign affairs? Those are two questions which might be discussed under this vote. It has been said that we are not to have all the facts in this matter, but I Believe the government would be well advised to have our defence policy wrapped up with that of the mother country on land, on sea and in the air. The defence policy of a dominion such as Canada should be fashioned after and coordinated with that of Great Britain. The government has announced that it was not consulted but advised by the British government in connection with foreign policy, a distinction without a difference. The reason may have been that it did not want to be consulted; some have said that. The government says it has simply been advised. The distinction between " advised " and " consulted " may be a play on words.
We have no defence force. Would we wait to advise and consult the mother country if an enemy were to come here? No; we would be glad to advise or consult then, because we would not want this country to be overrun by an enemy dictator. Never in the history of Canada has it been more necessary than it is now to tell the Canadian people the exact state of affairs. There is no use in depending upon pan-Americanism and the Monroe doctrine. We have depended upon them in the past, and they have been found wanting. We owe all the freedom and liberty we have to the motherland, and are entirely dependent upon her for defence and freedom.
Our policy of defence, in all its detail, is wrapped up with that of the mother country. As I understand the defence policy of Canada, it must be wrapped up with that of Great

Britain. Our defence policy is wrapped up in Locarno, and in the League of Nations. Our policy is one of isolation. If Canada's reliance is on the League of Nations, then it is leaning on a broken reed, because the league is bankrupt. The policy of Woodrow Wilson, that of open diplomacy, is a sham and has gone forever. This is the tenth league of nations that civilization has witnessed. They have all proposed through a formula to prevent war. They would have stopped war two thousand years ago, if a formula was all that was needed, but never in the history of the world have they been able to do so. There have been leagues of nations before, throughout the civilized world, and they have been complete failures. If a league of nations was sufficient to prevent war, then former leagues would have stopped wars two thousand years ago.
Is Canada still a member of the league? If the league is in existence, for what purpose is it? Our expenditures in connection with the league are very great.
In regard to the vote we are now considering for national defence I would call attention to the law of Canada to-day as it appears in section 63 of the Militia Act, chapter 132 of the revised statutes, which states:
The militia or any part thereof, or any officer or man thereof, may be called out for any military purpose other than drill or training, at such times and in such manner as is prescribed.
Then section 64:
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
Then section 66 gives the governor in council these further powers:
Whenever the governor in council places the militia, or any part thereof, on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within fifteen days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
The is the law of Canada to-day. In the belief that armies, navies and air forces were unnecessary, the politicians led Great Britain to disarm. That disarmament came about through the agitation of pacifists, the League of Nations and other agents of separatism. Great Britain was led to disarm in 1922. She had the finest army, the finest air force and the finest navy the world had ever seen, all of which she scrapped. The great peace mother

Since 1933 the Japanese have captured Manchuria; Italy has taken Ethiopia, and Germany has invaded the Rhine and Austria. Despots and dictators with armed forces that were illegal, the world over have been looking at Canada with covetous eyes. This great, rich country, with its magnificent natural resources and wide open spaces has been coveted the world over. To-day within the empire we are at the parting of the ways. An unarmed Great Britain or an unarmed empire invites invasion, insult and finally extinction. There is no better or more certain way to war than to have an unarmed British Empire, an unarmed Great Britain.
There is an old Italian proverb which says, "The world will always stand aside to let anyone pass who knows where he is going." These dictators know where they are going. We might have had them here in Canada. Do we know where Canada is going? The world let Hitler go where he is going to claim world hegemony and dictatorship. Some hon. members to the left, in and out of the house, a year ago were willing to depend upon the Monroe doctrine and pan-Americanism for our defence. If they followed that for a few more days they would soon know whither Hitler and other dictators were going. Canada faces in time not only the possibility but a strong probability of invasion.
We do not know where Canada and the dominions are going. We are just where we were a hundred years ago. We have no adequate defence force to protect our borders. We have been outdistanced by Italy and Germany. Another mistake was this: We spent $3,500,000 on the League of Nations; in order to please the league and to please the United States we quarrelled with Italy. I say it was not worth the loss of a boy scout to send a defence force to Ethiopia, or to quarrel with Italy, once one of our most devoted allies. It is a great stroke of good fortune that Great Britain's Prime Minister has now seen fit to 'bring these two old allies closer together.
As I said the other night, in connection with the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the dissolution of the Japanese alliance brought great danger to the Pacific coast. I have no quarrel with Japan. I shall not say a word against a country which has been our devoted ally. If we had stuck to our policy in the far east we would
be much better off in the Pacific to-day and have retained the Japanese alliance. We would have been much better off if we had given-our money, through the mother country, towards the maintenance of the great Singapore-base, a naval base established for the protection of Canadian, New Zealand and Australian interests in the Pacific. Australia and New Zealand have given about $5,000,000 towards the construction of that base. It was a project which would have protected us in. the Pacific.
It is too bad that in order to please the United States we lost an opportunity to keep our alliance with Japan, and to please a section of the people in South Africa and Ireland we consented to that lamentable act, the Statute of Westminster. We have seen the results of such a policy in what has happened' in the far east. We are depending upon the United States to keep order in the far east when we should be ready to cooperate with the motherland in her alliance with Japan there.
We are now realizing some of the mistakes that have been made. We have sided with the south of Ireland and South Africa in certain matters, and India has been given over to Gandhi through this policy of lack of preparation and pacifism. Because of the disarmed condition of Great Britain and the dominions, the British Empire was on the verge of war only a month ago.
In my opinion the league of nations' society is doing a great deal of harm in Canada. The British Broadcasting Corporation in Great Britain has stopped pacifist harangues over the air. They have been stopped in the United States and they should be stopped here. These people are hoping for the millennium described by Tennyson, but we cannot hope to escape the horrors of war on our own soil unless we have some force behind us. Great Britain was the only large country that stood by the League of Nations and promoted peace; the others all got out while the going was good. Great Britain disarmed and France disarmed, and as soon as there was complete disarmament by Britain and France, Germany, when fully armed crossed the Rhine and occupied the Rhineland. If the league had been any good at all it would have stopped that invasion. That was one-great mistake which was made. But France was disunited and disarmed, without a proper government and with communism rampant, and Germany stole a march on her and is still marching in Europe.
What we need to-day is another George Canning, and I think we have one in the present Prime Minister of Great Britain to.

keep us out of European wars. The league Shas done more to provoke war than to avert it. It has been a source of mischief ever since its creation. The United States . would not even join it. We see the result of all this in a vote of $34,000,000 to be paid by the taxpayers of Canada for all this folly. One of our great Anglican bishops in England said the other day that the civilization of Europe is not worth preserving; that it is worse now than it was a thousand years ago.
A few years ago Mr. John Buchan was then a member of the British House of Commons. He had an almost uncanny knack of interpreting public opinion, and he certainly expressed the view of the vast majority of his fellow countrymen when he said "that the League of Nations and the league of nations' society were largely in the hands of the crank, the sentimentalist and that appalling creature, the publicist." I hope the government of the day will stop considering the voices of the pacifists in this country as the voices of all the people of Canada. They are not. They have had their day and generation and we have seen the results. The government should not mistake the babble of the pacifists for the voice of the people of Canada on foreign affairs and on the question of adequate defence nor the voice of the Isolationists.
I hope the minister will not think I am criticizing his estimates as I am not. First, I should like to refer to Camp Borden. During the war a large air camp was established at this point. There are four landing fields, and I think the camp is unsurpassed in Canada for natural drainage and the facilities offered for landing and taking off. This camp has now been to some extent abandoned for Trenton, where under the best of conditions it is not considered safe to train young pilots. I know some changes have been made during the past year at Camp Borden, but I would *direct attention to the fact that a large number of young men were killed at Deseronto during the war because of the winds prevailing in that part of the country. I consider *Camp Borden as being a more satisfactory place for large air force training of pilots. I have talked over this matter with men who ihave been there and they agree with me.
The signal corps has been transferred from Borden to Kingston where the training conditions are rather inadequate. When Sir Frederick Borden was minister of militia there was a great artillery camp at Petawawa. This was considered one of the finest artillery camps in the empire, and many generals have commented upon it. I think we should have something like that at Camp Borden, Niagara

and in all the provinces. Niagara should be used to a greater extent. Thousands of dollars should be spent on the Stanley barracks at Toronto, on old quarters and better quarters. These barracks have a historical interest and they should be retained.
I am sorry the government has not brought down a more definite policy with regard to the Pacific. We might have had a Locarno in the Pacific with Japan, England, Russia and the United States, but owing to the breaking of the Japanese alliance that was not brought about. I believe we would have better protection in a naval way on the Pacific if we were more closely allied with the motherland. We should take a greater interest in the Singapore base instead of leaving the matter of Pacific defence to the mother country and Australia and New Zealand.
There has been a definite change in our defence policy since the Statute of Westminster was passed. That statute was passed to please southern Ireland and South Africa, and the result is that New Zealand, Australia, Canada and all the other dominions are considered as separate countries which can make war or negotiate treaties. That folly called separatism divides us in war and separates us in peace. These countries have a separate defence policy from that of the motherland, and on the whole I believe the statute was a great mistake on the part of the dominions.
More consideration should be given to air defences. There is not only the possibility but a great probability that air raids will occur in the next war in which Canada is involved. The defence of our population from air raids should be considered. These raids will be the chief source of danger in all future wars, and we shall be living in a false paradise if we do not adopt measures to protect ourselves. Abyssinia was recently a theatre of war, and we all know the destruction of civilian population that occurred through this means of attack. Abyssinia is an open country with only a small density of population as compared with what there is on the island of Montreal and in other parts of Canada, and yet great damage resulted.
Air raids can work great havoc in time of war, and the menace will be a very real one in Canada, especially to the people of Quebec, the maritimes and British Columbia. I am glad that some preparation, although it may be only a beginning, has already been made by the minister to meet this danger. I know he has been out looking over the camps. A fleet of aircraft could pass up the Ottawa river without a moment's notice and blow up these buildings, the Chateau Laurier, the

Supply-National Defence
railway station and other large buildings. We should have very little warning of the approaching attack. Consultation and advice are words that are much used by the government nowadays, but we would not be consulted about any air raids that were contemplated against Canada. The enemy's aircraft would be upon us before you could say " 0 Canada," or sing God Save the King. An aerial bombardment is one of the dangers most to be apprehended in time of war, particularly in large cities with their dense populations; the protection of cities from aerial bombardment should be one of the chief objectives of the national defence department, and proper equipment for defence against this menace should be provided. Probably the minister will have something to say about that later on.
Large quantities of poisonous gas could easily be spread over a large area as was done in Abyssinia, and incendiary bombs dropped on our large cities, with great destruction and slaughter, and the enemy aircraft could get back to their base in practically no time. These attacks would not only bring ruin to our cities and towns but break the morale of our people and prevent us from developing a proper defence and mobilizing our man power and armaments.
In regard to foreign and defence affairs Canada should wake up out of its slumber before it is too late. We were just as near war a month ago as we were in July, 1914. We were told last August at lake Simcoe, Ontario, that war was gone forever; but here in the month of March this association with a high-sounding name, the Canadian Institute of Economics and Politics, received a very rude awakening. Pacifists and economists have had their day in Canada and the United States, and have failed. Real science, rightly understood, was the admiration of the world, but the way in which science has been applied with its inventions to making war more terrible has made science a curse to civilization.
In conclusion, I want to say a word or two about the schools and the way in which false and injurious information has been disseminated throughout Canada by many agencies in regard particularly to the League of Nations, defence, foreign affairs and the cadet movement. The cadet movement is not a military movement; it is more for physical training. I understand that the minister has been taking some steps along the line of having a national policy, a volunteer one in Canada for home service and home defence of all kinds. That is not a luxury but a necessity. I notice that the British Field Marshal Lord Milne, on January 7 last, was talking about this problem as it relates to the schools. He was addressing
the secondary school teachers in England, and I am glad that the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is going to address next Saturday the high schools of the city of Toronto. Lord Milne said:
Sometimes too much was made of learning when reference was made to education. Character, patriotism and discipline were equally important.
An article in the January, 1938, issue of the National Review at page 48 quotes the head master of a public school as saying:
A man may obtain a double-first and yet be uneducated.
The writer of the article makes this comment:
Conversely, one has known educated men who could neither read nor write. Until the Board of Education insists that formation of character, the obligations of duty, patriotism and self-sacrifice are the mainsprings of education, young men will be found wanting, when put to a practical test, in the responsibilities of citizenship. . . .
I have already commented on the lack of state teaching on the duties of citizenship, including service for one's country; but what is to be said of authorities in state-aided universities and schools who openly inculcate the principle of peace at any price?
Are we doing our duty and teaching the principles which Lord Milne advocated?

Mr. Chairman, I followed with great interest the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond). He has his opinion, and I have mine. My only regret is that they do not harmonize any more. For instance, I could not help noticing these words in the latter part of his speech which I quote from memory: "I am not prompted by blind confidence nor by systematic distrust."
I hope my hon. friend will not be offended when I tell him that neither are these the feelings which prompted hon. members to oppose an increase in military expenditures. They did it on principle just like the hon. member last session, and as they do it now, as a matter of conviction. I may add that I have never questioned for a moment the fine purposes of my colleagues who did not share my views on this important question of policy.
It is not because they were impregnated with blind confidence that the majority of my colleagues in this house voted for the defence estimates. Neither was it on account of a systematic distrust that we took a different view. Did not the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), Who is liberal
Supply-National Defence

and wide-minded, state on several occasions, and particularly at the recent demonstration tendered the hon. member for Ottawa-East (Mr. Pinard) that the Liberal party hated coercion which is necessarily derived from narrow-mindedness.
Mr. Chairman, the events which took place throughout the world since the last session of this parliament and the threats of war which are hanging over central Europe at the present time would not justify my change of attitude as regards military expenditures. Last year, while we were discussing the defence estimates in committee, I asked the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) on several occasions if he would require a larger sum every year. As a matter of fact, I foresaw the expenditures which we are now discussing. Although they were reduced by $2,000,000, these estimates for the present fiscal year still amount to $34,034,364.42. Therefore I am quite determined once again to oppose this increase in the expenditure for militia and defence, in order to revert to the figure set for that purpose in the 1936-37 estimates. Why? Because the present estimates are still $18,155,953 higher than those for 1936-37.
In the compiling of those figures I have taken into account the amount of $2,201,000 for the purchase of two destroyers by the Canadian government, which appeared in the supplementary estimates for 1937. There is another reason why I should continue my fight. Canada, although far removed from the horrors of the Far East, the Iberian Peninsula and Central Europe, must realize what a suicide she would keep in store for herself for the day when, going beyond her own borders, she would take part in a foreign war. Our country will grow peacefully and harmoniously only in so far as it keeps its eyes on its own people, on its immense natural resources, on its youth whose strength must be preserved for the furthering of the progress of Canada and of Canada only, of its industries, its trade, its agriculture which has saved it from bankruptcy, which has fed the children, the women and the men of Canada. Our country must have peace to prosper on this American continent which witnessed its birth, its growth and its attainment of nationhood. Let us be guided by our traditions of strength and courage. Let these traditions bind us forever and more exclusively to this Canadian land of ours, the sole object of our love, hope and admiration.
In conclusion, I would like to state that, in the account I have just made of a situation which I find alarming, I had no other idea in
[Mr. Lacombe.l
mind, I was animated with no other motive than an ardent desire to serve my country while being of service to my constituents. I know their views, I know that they are inspired by a truly Canadian spirit. Therefore I would consider myself false to my trust if I took an opposite attitude.
Mr. Chairman, it is very painful for me again to differ on this vital matter with statesmen whom I respect, whose talent, ability and courage I admire. But I cannot sacrifice to the noble sentiments of friendship and admiration firm beliefs, or an ideal and a mentality which the horrors of war have irrevocably anchored in my mind and my heart. Others will perhaps criticize me. Nevertheless I will stand indomitably, with my eyes fixed on the firm, clear and limpid manifestation of principles dear to my heart, while respecting the convictions of my fellow members.
Let me add just one word. There is not a single Canadian citizen worthy of the name who would want the ruin of Canada. Well, any new military adventure on our part outside our own territory would involve tremendous expenses from which we would never recover. What I want to avoid is the bankruptcy and the downfall of my country. That is what I will oppose with all my strength. That is what I will condemn to my last breath.
Far removed from the maddened old world, and from a civilization bordering on barbarism, let us live in peace at home. Let us concentrate all our energies upon the attainment of the destinies of a great nation where tomorrow will blossom forth the virile beauty of a great people.
The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie stated at the beginning of his remarks, if I remember rightly, that he had not received from the Minister of National Defence in the course of the last session a satisfactory answer regarding the limits of Canada. Mr. Chairman, in my humble opinion, Canada's limits are clearly determined by the Canadian Militia Act. I had no intention of speaking on this subject; I have been impelled to do so by the turn taken by the debate. I wish to tell the truth, the whole truth, as I see it, and to be corrected if I am wrong. The Militia Act of Canada, chapter 132 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, volume III, section 64, page 2789 contains the following provision respecting active service.
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.

Now let us see what section 69 of the same act says, on page 2790:
The Army Act for the time being in force in Great Britain, the king's regulations, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this act or the regulations made hereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia.
I find nothing in the amendments brought to the Militia Act since 1927, that purports to repeal the sections that I have just quoted. True, there is chapter 21 of the Statutes of Canada for 1932-33, 23-24 George V, page 97, which was sanctioned on April 12, 1933. But this act refers only to forces of His Majesty from other parts of the British commonwealth or from a colony when visiting the Dominion of Canada. On the other hand, section 6 of the same act leaves wide discretion to the governor in council, particularly subsection 2, page 102, which reads as follows:
The governor in council
(i)	may attach temporarily to a home force any member of another force to which this section applies who is .placed at his disposal for the purpose by the service authorities of that part of the commonwealth to which the other force belongs;
(ii)	subject to anything to the contrary in the conditions applicable to his service, may place any member of a home force at the disposal of the service authorities of another part of the commonwealth for the purpose of being attached temporarily by those authorities to a force to which this section applies belonging to that part of the commonwealth.
Then, section 8, page 103, provides as follows:
So far as regards any naval force and the members of any such force, the provisions of this act shall be deemed to be in addition to and not in derogation of such of the provisions of any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom or of the parliament of any other part of the commonwealth as are for the time being applicable to that force and the members thereof.
I shall close, Mr. Speaker, with another quotation from the Militia Act of Canada:
All the male inhabitants of Canada, of the age of eighteen years and upwards, and under sixty, not exempt or disqualified by law, and being British subjects, shall be liable to service in the militia: provided that the governor general may require all the male inhabitants of Canada, capable of bearing arms, to serve in the case of a levee en masse.
Be it understood, Mr. Chairman, that in making these quotations I am not moved by bitterness towards any one. I feel that, in speaking as I did, I am fulfilling the trust placed in me by my constituents on October 14, 1935. On nomination day, that is October 7, 1935, at a great meeting attended by more than 12,000 voters of both sexes, I was asked
this question: "What will be your attitude in the matter of military appropriations?" I replied: "I will speak against them in the House of Commons and vote against them." Indeed, I stated this fact in the course of the observations that I made in this house last year. The profound convictions I hold in this matter, Mr. Chairman, make it impossible for me to change my attitude. This is my final word.

BRADETTE (Cochrane) (Translation): Mr. Chairman, before proceeding with what I have to say on this very important question, I wish to congratulate the hon. the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) for the splendid speech which he delivered a moment ago, when he set forth the whole situation before the House of Commons and the country so far as national defence is concerned. Of course, it required a great deal of courage on the part of the dominion government, last year, when he decided to carry on with the system of national defence which we had in this country, and which, on account of financial stress, during years of depression, had to be left more or less impaired. We very well remember the commotion brought about throughout the country by the announcement that the dominion government would spend for national defence purposes a sum of $36,034,371.42 during the fiscal year of 1937-38. Every member of this house remembers the discussions that took place about it. They also remember the controversy which was waged by newspapers of every political shade throughout the country. These press comments showed that the people realized that the government had displayed great courage under the circumstances, and appreciated the necessity of such a policy.
Once again the government is asking us to vote a considerable sum to carry out this national defence plan which was inaugurated last year.
Of course, there is not one citizen worthy of being called a Canadian, whether he come from the east, the west or the central part of Canada, who would dare say that he is not in favour of peace. However, Mr. Chairman, our people must, of necessity, be practical.
No doubt, Canada built great hopes on the League of Nations, which I am sure, has not yet completed the great task which it had mapped out, namely that of maintaining international peace in every part of the civilized world. We realize however the great difficulties which the League of Nations has to face. Again I say that I do not believe

there is one man in Canada, whatever may be his race, religion, or political faith, who does not seek peace not only in Canada but in the whole world. But we must realize how serious present conditions are. There is no doubt that Canada is ideally situated as regards national defence. Mr. Chairman, there are in my own constituency, just as there are likely in all parts of Canada, thousands of returned soldiers who took part in the great war of 1914-18. They risked their lives for what they consider to be the cause of humanity and peace. After the war, they returned to their activities, and they now have sons old enough to serve in the army. I know that they are just as anxious as anybody else not to see their sons enduring the sacrifices which they went through or witnessing the same horrors which were their lot for four years. Mr. Chairman, I have listened attentively to the masterly speech delivered this afternoon 'by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). He stated 
that public opinion, in connection with defence, could be divided into five groups. We are sure of one thing at least, and it is that nobody in particular, no political party can boast of being alone against war. We all agree as to that, in Canada. That is why, recently and in certain circumstances, some members of parliament or certain parts of the population seem to assume the whole responsibility in avoiding war.
The Minister of National Defence briefly referred to the signification of nationalism and its possible results. The Larousse dictionary defines the word as follows:
Marked preference for anything pertaining to one's nation.
Undoubtedly all persons forming a country must belong to it, not in a sectional or provincial sense, but in a strictly national sense with all that the word implies. That is one reason why there should be no opposition to the appropriations for national defence, because, after all, when establishing a home or a business, one must accept all the responsibilities of that new situation. When young and living under our father's roof we do not realize our responsibilities. By the Statute of Westminster, Canada became an individual nation in the British commonwealth of nations, which means new responsibilities, national as well as international. To be fair in the circumstances, the least we can do is to be prepared to defend ourselves.
Before six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I briefly referred to our geographical and national position on the north American continent. Fortunately for us, our neighbour to the south is a friendly nation, on whose cooperation we may rely for a great number of years. We are separated by a 3,000 mile boundary line along which there is not a single fortress, and where peace prevails.
This afternoon, the Pan-American Federation was mentioned several times. That reminded us of the famous Monroe doctrine so often quoted by those who are opposed to any increase in our national defence appropriations. What is the meaning of these words: the Monroe doctrine? They mean that the United States told the nations of the world that any attempt to conquer countries in North or South America or to interfere with their administration, would be considered as unfriendly acts. Let us suppose that Canada should decide to abandon its national defence-as was suggested on a number of occasions in certain parts of Canada- the responsibility would then fall on the shoulders of the American nation. Would it be fair? Let us go a step further. Let us

Supply-National Defence
imagine Canada being invaded by a foreign power without possessing any means of defence. Then, the American people, according to the Monroe doctrine, would be forced to protect us, because they would not want a foreign nation to secure a footing in Canada. Would not the Americans, who are a practical people, after defending us with success I suppose and after spending vast sums of money and sacrificing a great number of human lives, ask us to pay the cost if we had the desire of maintaining our national existence? It being so, we must realize that those who mention the Monroe doctrine are not on solid grounds when they say that we have no need to defend ourselves but that the responsibility belongs to the great nation to the south. We have to study this matter from all angles, Mr. Chairman. As I have already said, we are proud of our new status as part of the British commonwealth of nations. But that status does not go without responsibilities and one of them is surely to take the means of protecting our own borders and our coast line in case of attack.
Many people ask us: "Against whom are we arming?" We all know that Great Britain wants peace and is not looking for further conquests. Great Britain wants to maintain peace, not only in Europe but throughout the civilized world. Is France actually getting ready for a war of conquest? No, Mr. Chairman, France only wants to defend her frontiers and protect her homes, because she still remembers the two invasions she was subjected to during the last sixty years. The same may be said of the United States, where a billion dollars was voted for the navy only a few days ago. Against whom are the United States arming? Are they arming against Canada or against the nations of South America or Asia? No, Mr. Chairman, they are not arming for attack, they are arming for defence in case of attack. That is how I understand the situation and how it should be understood generally in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I am not in a position to say, and I would not go so far as to claim that I am thoroughly familiar with the feelings of the people in Quebec. However, may I be allowed to quote a short article by Mr. Eugene L'Heureux, published in L'Action Catholique a year ago, when the estimates for national defence were under consideration in the house?
I think that this article sets forth quite correctly the general feeling of the majority . of the people in the province of Quebec.
It is as follows:
For Canada Only
Actual conditions, however, must be taken into account. Lack of knowledge in matters of national defence organization deters us from passing judgment on the appropriations sought by the government for the organization of the country's defence. We think it possible to place confidence in the government on that score, all the more so as the Prime Minister has emphasized the purely Canadian destination of this military expenditure.
In such times as these, when danger threatens from all sides, even the most peace-loving nations feel the need of protection against the possible tragic outcome of domestic trouble as well as against colonial ambitions of the great powers. Under present conditions, Canada's armament budget may appear reasonable event in the eyes of the anti-militarists.
Approaching the question from the point of view of French Canadians, we think that instead of bemoaning these military expenditures (under present conditions), they should rather endeavour to occupy a prominent place in the country's armed forces, so as to partake fully of the nation's activities and to claim their full share even in the military domain, and also to find in military life the benefit of a certain discipline in which they are lacking, much to our general and oft expressed regret.
I consider this article quite logical and I know whereof I speak for the following reasons. I had the honour last spring to take part, in the province of Quebec, my native province, in a by-election campaign, during which I made it my duty to discuss in the Gaspe peninsula the national defence appropriations. I must say that the explanations I gave on that occasion were very closely followed by the electors who fully realized the soundness of voting these appropriations for the defence of their own country.
What are the other nations of the British commonwealth doing? This afternoon's newspapers tell us that Australia is to spend in the space of three years nearly 145 million dollars for its own defence. Has Australia any thought of aggression, either in India, in Japan or elsewhere? No, Australia wishes only to defend her own coasts, her own boundaries. The same principle applies to South America and New Zealand, and that is the principle which should be applied to the appropriations we are now asked to vote.
These appropriations include a fairly large expenditure for aviation. Necessity compels us to develop financially and commercially, in respect of machinery, of modern invention, and so forth,
I surely believe that a military air force if put to proper use, would aid the development of the natural resources in the northern section of the dominion. When, in Canada, one looks at a map of the country, one is astonished to see a narrow strip of settled land, stretching from east to west. It seems that there is a
Supply-National Defence

certain desire to live as close as possible to the American border. If we want Canada to become a great nation, our expansion must necessarily be caried out in the northern part of the country, where a bountiful Providence endowed us with immense and untold resources still undeveloped. I am also of the opinion that a military aviation would provide an excellent agency for the development of the northern part of Canada in its entirety.
No one in these dark days is unmindful of the enormous burden meant by the conditions which we are now called upon to face. There is no one who, in his daily prayers does not ask for the maintenance of peace throughout the civilized world. In Europe, in Canada, in the United States and in the whole world, youth realizes the problem with which it is confronted at the present time. How one longs to see such noble dreams of peace come true, just as one wishes the establishment of the United States of Europe, such as was advocated by Aristide Briand, eminent French statesman. How I long, for my part, to see the people of South America, United States, Great Britain, Germany, Russia, Japan, in short, all the civilized nations of the world, formed into one great federation, constituting a solid group, a single nation, so that the world may never again know such tremendous sacrifice of human lives as was witnessed between 1914 and 1918, during the war which was supposed to end all wars. But twenty short years have elapsed since that awful conflagration, and yet the diplomats of Europe are once more wondering what the following day has in store, and are apprehensive as to the future.
Before concluding, I wish to thank the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the noble and national attitude he has taken. During that critical situation, he was successful in not embroiling matters, and brought home the seriousness of the problem, not only to parliament, but to the people of Canada. I feel also, that I should express my opinion concerning the position taken by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Chamberlain, who showed us that one must keep a steady head in these momentous hours and whose desire is that the problem which the European nations are facing at the present time may find their solution in peace. I also wish to extend my congratulations to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). Indeed, it would mean a loss of faith in our civilization if the solution of these problems were to be secured only through the destruction of millions of young lives and by delaying the march of civilization. I pray to God that all men may work

in cooperation towards the solution of these problems, so that the tremendous sacrifices of 1914-1918 may be spared, not only to our country, but to the whole world, and it is my sincere wish that they may not be witnessed again by the present generation, otherwise it would be, unquestionably, the dawn of a new era of decadence.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to attempt to compete with hon. members who have spoken respecting matters of national policy, in an attempt to evaluate the foreign policies of this country or of Great Britain, or of the circumstances obtaining in the world to-day. I have listened with great interest and, indeed, a marked measure of enthusiasm to the speech delivered this afternoon in this chamber by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), when he set forth a report of the situation with respect to the technical and mechanical developments of the problem of defence in Canada.
For the little time I propose to take tonight it is my desire to speak about another phase of our problem. I should like to direct attention to the situation which obtains in Canada to-day with respect to the man whom I may call the man behind the gun-the man who is a member of the permanent force. It is not my intention, nor have I the ability, to launch into an oratorical description of the position in which these all too few men find themselves, nor shall I deal with the question in a manner calculated to arouse either the enthusiasm or the passion of this house on behalf of these men. Within the constituency which I have the honour to represent is located one of the larger military districts. During my short tenure of office I have taken it upon myself to study, in some measure at least, the conditions under which these men serve their country. These men have behind them the same traditions as are behind you and me, and many of them took up army life as a career at a time when it was more of a career than it is at present. I am ready to confess that many of our young men would have been glad of the opportunity during the last few unfortunate years to enter the service of this country and find even the kind of security obtainable under such circumstances.
In the brief time which I shall allow myself I intend to refer to four or five phases of the conditions under which these gentlemen serve their country, my country and your country. I shall make some representations to the minister, and through the minister to the government, for an improvement of the conditions under which these men serve.

Under date of March 10 of this year I read the following headline emanating from Great Britain:
Hore-Belisha's army estimates promise more attractive life for British soldier.
Less posture, polish, higher pay for Tommy.
I shall not deal to-night with either the posture or the polish as it concerns the enlisted man in Canada, but I want to point out that in the conditions obtaining in the world to-day the imperial government has seen fit to make a considerable effort to improve the lot of the enlisted man in the permanent forces of Great Britain. I think it is time that we should look at the picture that obtains in Canada and consider whether we cannot do something to attract to this service the type of young man who has a real contribution to make. I do not conceive it likely that in the immediate or near future we shall be maintaining in this country a military establishment on a large scale-I do not know that is even desirable-but in my opinion we should have a highly efficient military service. If we are to have that, then we must look to the condition of the enlisted man.
For my own convenience and the convenience of hon. members I propose to deal with some possible amendments to the Militia Act, without being technical in any way. I think in the minds of the men who serve us so loyally these amendments are considered to be advantageous, first of all for their own concern, second, for the government that employs them and, third, for all the Canadian citizens who support this establishment. For some period of time there has been considerable dissatisfaction with the exorbitant duty placed upon the importation of military kit from Great Britain. I appreciate the fact that this is not a matter which can be decided by the Minister of National Defence, but I have raised the question previously with other members of the administration. In putting forth this suggestion I am thinking more particularly of the men in the non-permanent force. My description of the non-permanent force is a force in which a man puts up his own money for the privilege of serving his country. Under these circumstances it seems to me that any representations by the Minister of National Defence to the council generally might well be listened to.
There is another condition obtaining in the permanent force to which I should like to direct attention. For the past forty years there has been a practice in the British army, upon which our Canadian permanent force is modelled, of making an allowance to a married man for his children. It is pretty
well established, even in military life, that two cannot live as cheaply as one, since an allowance, I believe of fifty cents per day, is made to the married man who has no children. No ration, allowance is made for the minor children of a soldier in the permanent forces, and I suggest to the minister that he consider the possibility of making some allowance in this connection. Allowances are made in Great Britain for children under the age of sixteen, and a suggestion has been made that in this country an allowance should be made for boys under the age of sixteen and girls under the age of eighteen years. In order to get this thing started I would be quite happy to have these allowances made under the same conditions as prevail in Great Britain.
There is another matter which I think the minister, and through him the government, might very well take into consideration. I believe that a portion of a pension due to a man who has served his time in the permanent militia should accrue to his widow when he predeceases her. At the present time a man serves a minimum of sixteen years, I believe, at the end of which time ,he may retire on pension. If he predeceases his wife, she receives no pension and in many instances becomes a charge upon the state. It seems to me that in trying to make the service attractive, we should consider doing something in this regard. When the spirit is upon us and we are prepared to do something about defence, we should enlarge this matter of pensions. The estate of the average enlisted man consists of his pay while in service and his pension after his service is completed, and I know of case after case where hardship has resulted. I shall not at this juncture recite individual cases as I believe that most hon. members who have had any connection with the permanent force will have personal knowledge of many cases of men who have retired on pension and then shortly after have passed away, and we have had the spectacle of the wife who has been the sustaining partner of her husband through a long period of service having to go on relief or being left to the charity of friends.
I had intended to develop that; but I pass on to another consideration, and this is one which particularly affects single men in the service. It is well known to hon. members that the enlisted man in the permanent force, whether he comes from Halifax or Vancouver or Winnipeg or Montreal, must serve in the military district to which he is sent; he has no choice in the matter. From time to time these. men earn a certain furlough, and a peculiar situation obtains in that regard. If a man who is to-day a member of or who has retired on pension from the permanent

force of Canada goes to Great Britain, he is afforded the courtesy of half fare on the railways of the motherland, just as that half fare is accorded to members of the permanent force of Great Britain itself. But the only men enlisted in the service of Canada who,
I am informed, enjoy a similar privilege on Canadian railways, are the ratings in the naval service, and for a long time this has been a sore point with enlisted men in this country. I have in mind a couple of chaps who enlisted in the permanent force of Canada in the city of Halifax and were subsequently transferred to the city of Winnipeg. After an honourable and somewhat extended service they earned a furlough, and their natural desire was to return to their homes in the city of Halifax. What do we find? We find that there is at the present time no provision in the Militia Act to accord these chaps the consideration they would be accorded if they were members of the British force or if they were naval ratings or for any reason wished to take their furlough in the British Isles. I would commend to the consideration of the minister and the government the placing of our own Canadian enlisted men in at least as advantageous a position in Canada in this respect as when they go overseas as guests of the mother country.
Turning to the subject of living and working conditions, I was gratified to hear the minister speak to-day of the advancement in technical and mechanical devices in the defence forces of this country. I have had the experience of seeing service in a theatre of war, and I came away from that with a definite impression that the most important military detail in any army is the man who is described, as I said a few moments ago, as the man behind the gun. It may be the man behind the gun or in an aeroplane or in a unit of the military forces that serve at the front. It is the hope of this government and of all governments that our permanent force shall be the nucleus of whatever forces, defensive or otherwise, it may be necessary in the future to raise; that it shall be an inspiration and educative force for whatever forces it may be necessary to mobilize.
Certain conditions obtaining to-day in Canada with respect to the living and service conditions of these men do not commend themselves to me and will not, I think, commend themselves to hon. members who have knowledge of what is taking place. About three years ago I had occasion to look into the circumstances surrounding the living conditions of married men on the strength but not on the married men's establishment; that is to say, men who had married without

official permission. Those with any military experience know the vast difference between official permission and just plain ordinary permission. In the one case you have the support of the law in all its majesty; but in the other the law forgets its majesty, and says: If you get married, we will look the other way. To the enlisted man there is not anything like the same difference as there is to the official mind. Consequent upon representations being made, a serious attempt was made by the minister, and, I am bound to say, by the deputy minister, as well as, I hope, by certain officials of the department, to remedy the situation, which is far from satisfactory. I found and others have found that men who had served six, nine or twelve years satisfactorily but who had married without permission were not being reenlisted, but on the contrary were being thrown on the unemployed market without any consideration. I made certain representations to the minister, as did others, and some definite steps were taken to remedy the situation, but I am sorry to say they have not worked out as advantageously as we had hoped. I am of the opinion that further investigation of this matter might result in advantage both to the department and to the men who are most interested.
There are certain other considerations. Dealing with these men who have married without official permission and reverting to Winnipeg, part of which I represent, and in which constituency the headquarters of military district No. 10 is situated, I found on investigation that with respect to every building under the Department of National Defence in that city occupied by soldiers or by officials or officers of the department, a special additional allowance of twenty per cent was made for heating because of the building being located in the city of Winnipeg. This fuel allowance, I am told, does not apply to members of the forces who for any reason whatsoever maintain their residence outside the official barracks, and I would suggest to the minister that he seriously canvass the possibility of relieving the plight of these men. In some instances the men are entitled to be on the married strength but are unable to get suitable quarters, and they are forced to buy their own furniture and to go to considerable extra expense by living outside the barracks.
Finally, I should like to say a word or two about the question of married men not on the married strength, and by that I mean those who married without the official sanction of the department. I have investigated not merely one or two or three, but many of these

cases. I have gone to the trouble to request from the department-and in every instance my request has been courteously granted- the military record, length of service, and kind of qualifications which these men possess. I have also gone not once but many times to the barracks and inspected the quarters in some detail, and I know the situation which obtains there. I wonder if, in view of . the stress which we are now inclined to place upon the question of defence, and in view of the clearly established importance of the men who constitute the first line of our defence, the minister might not consider now, at this session, the possibility of making some allowance and recognizing to some extent these marriages without official consent. I wonder if the minister has considered making an allowance of, say sixty per cent of the marriage allowance to these married men outside barracks until such time as they can come properly on the married strength, because on this question I feel that the department is or has been to no small degree responsible for a condition which obtains very largely in my own constituency.
For a number of years we have followed the practice of enlisting men in the permanent force and putting them in barracks in the very districts from which they come; and I suggest that it has been the tendency in the last seven or eight lean years to consider enlistment in the permanent force of Canada not so much in the light of a career as in the light of a job. When you take a young man of eighteen or nineteen, enlist him in the service and keep him in the district in which he was born, raised and educated, and so make no effort to change his environment, are you astonished that many of these young men come to regard the service as a job and their pay as wages just as much as though they were working for a private company, or that they begin to think before long of the possibility of maintaining a home of their own on that income, take a chance with a good-natured officer or one who conveniently looks the other way-as they all do-and so begin on that basis to build up something which they can ill afford to maintain? Perhaps, if we had used a little more foresight-and this consideration goes 'back further than three or four years-if we had trained at Halifax those who enlisted at Winnipeg, and at Vancouver those who enlisted at Halifax, and thereby completely broken the whole tenor and trend of their associations and their existence and brought them to think of the service as a career, this situation would not have arisen.
It was on these points particularly that I wished to present views which are not only my own but are shared- by a great many who have interested themselves in the welfare of these men. On their behalf, and in the interests of the kind of service in Canada for which I hope, I recommend to the minister and to the government consideration of these particular points.

I did at the time give a few reasons why I could not support that new departure which, in my opinion, was ill-timed and dangerous.
This year, the military estimates which have been brought down are practically as large as those of last year. Having regard to various opinions expressed in the course of the debate which took place last year, having regard also to subsequent international as well as national events, I intend to deal briefly with this policy of increased expenditure for the purpose of military reorganization.
I do not think I need state again that, in dealing with that question, I intend to dismiss every personal consideration, and to be guided only by an eager desire to deal with this question on its merits. In order to clear up any misapprehension in the matter I must state that I have no grievance against the government; on the contrary, I am on the most friendly terms with my leaders. Although I approve of Liberal policies and although I have a high regard, as I think I should, for views and opinions held by the administration, I shall take the liberty, on this matter of rearmament, of discussing frankly and honestly two basic features of Canadian defence; the military estimates and the delimitation of our boundaries.
I maintained in 1937 that neither our geographical position, our political situation, nor our financial circumstances warranted the increased estimates of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). After this period of one year, let us ascertain whether anything has occurred which might in any way alter the problem.
I am aware of no changes in our geographical position which offers us an exceptional degree of protection on all sides. On the east, we are separated from Europe by the Atlantic ocean; on the west there is, by virtue of the Pacific ocean, such a tremen-

The question of autonomy is also involved. Canada has gained her autonomy, or what we call by that name, after lengthy struggles on the part of Canadian statesmen of both parties. In these difficult times, it is more important than ever that we should not retrograde, we must not lose ground. Opinions are divided on this subject and some people are so blind to Canadian autonomy that they would not speak otherwise if they still had colonial status. While repeating that Canada is a free and sovereign country, they want us to place our sovereignty and our liberty at the service of the Empire, in other words to enslave our liberty.
Prior to last year, Canada had maintained a prudent peaceful policy. Not content with vague humanitarian principles, she had shown the way in the betterment of international relations. I proudly support that policy. If I opposed an increase in military expenditures last year, it is because I was sorry to see our country join in the armament race. Are we not committing ourselves further in 1938? Could not that armament policy be interpreted as the forsaking by Canada of the wish for peace that we have been proclaiming for so many years? Would that not lead nervous, restless and suspicious nations to believe that we are following in the wake of some large powers towards a policy of armed peace? Who can fail to see where that might lead us?
I am all the more frightened by the fact that our military boundaries are not yet defined. So long as they are not defined and so long as the other inconsistencies I have mentioned are not cleared up, I think I express the wish of the majority of my electors, in reserving my approval for such items of the military estimates which I think reasonable.

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length, but I feel there are one or two things I should like to say to-night. I think it would have been easier for -most if the statement by the minister had been made on one day and the debate proceeded with on some subsequent day. It was a lengthy address, and it did not seem to me clear. At one time the minister said we were preparing for the defence of Canada, and the defence of Canada only. At another moment we were hearing about the protection of Canada by the British fleet in the North sea. At another time we heard of the need which might arise for all democracies banding together once again to save democracy. It may be that in reading the speech it will be easier to understand the position of the minister than it was in listening to him. At any rate, after hearing it, and then listening to most of the speeches which followed, in a language which I am very sorry I do not understand, I find myself left entirely on my own resources, which possibly is the best place of all to be left. If we must fight another war to save democracy, we can be pretty sure that it will be the end of democracy. The one we fought to save democracy about half finished it, and another would be the end.
What we all feel, of course-and I do not feel it any more than other hon. members- is that it seems uncivilized to be able to find 836,000,000 or whatever it is we spend for defence, when, according to an authority on the schools in Saskatchewan, in that province we have thirty-five rural schools closed because money cannot be found with which to keep them open.. Yet we can find money to protect us from an enemy who was not named, although when the minister finished his speech I felt that the enemy would be here about next week. We can find money for defence; but we cannot find it to keep open the thirty-five schools in Saskatchewan, or for providing some sort of reasonable standard of living for almost, if not quite, a million people in Canada who are still on relief. When the minister waxed eloquent-and he was very eloquent, particularly at the end of his speech, about defending our homes-I was wondering just how eager the people who have been on relief for so long would be about defending their homes. I can understand that they would be eager to get into the army, but whether it would be in order to defend their homes or in order to obtain the assurance of something to eat and something for their families is another matter.

One cannot help being extremely sad that we seem, not in Canada so much as throughout the world, to be turning backward instead of progressing and going forward to a civilization in which things of the mind and the spirit count, and that in the very day when we are being freed from the necessity of arduous labour, when we could use the leisure thus created for the development of the art of living. The whole world apparently is providing itself with instruments of destruction, and again all in the name of peace. We are all arming in order that we may have peace. Never again shall I be fooled by that one. It may be true that we must arm; it may be true that we are all arming, but not to bring peace, because the more we arm the more likely it is that the days of peace are numbered and that before too long we shall have an opportunity of using the instruments of destruction which now so many nations are furiously building and gathering together.
Too, I cannot help feeling-and I am now thinking in the terms of democracies, from a Canadian point of view

that if we were as anxious for peace as the eloquent speeches on defence would have us think, we would have stopped sending to those countries that we believe would turn them into munitions, the material for the making of munitions. That is true of Canada, and true in a larger way of the British Commonwealth of Nations and the other great powers. I cannot understand a nation attempting to protect itself against the onslaught of another nation, and at the same time supplying it with the instruments of destruction which will be used against it. It simply does not make sense. When a few years ago these various nations seemed about to crack up, from a financial and economic point of view, the great powers came to their assistance and put them on their feet again, thus strengthening their enemies. We should have started sooner in the cause of peace and in a different way. It is important, at any rate to me, to see that none of the bullets which might come back in the bodies of the nationals of any country are made out of materials from our own land. Surely that is only a reasonable request, that we do nothing to arm an enemy, either by munitions or by loans. I cannot help thinking that if the great powers had been serious in this matter of peace, starting even twenty years ago or ten years ago, we could have avoided much of the difficulty which now threatens the whole world.
There is one other approach to peace which some time all nations will have to take. That is the approach which they will make in 51952-106J
their own countries, by financial or economic changes in each country which will remedy the difficulties within the nation and do something to lessen the suffering from poverty, in this day when we all know poverty should not exist.
I notice that the minister outlined the many schools of thought there are in this country, and, I think, very well, indeed. Personally I have changed from one to the other. I once thought that collectively we could act together, and in time could prevent the difficulty which now seems to threaten the world. I still think it could have been done. Now I feel-I am speaking more from instinct than anything else-more and more North American in my point of view, because less and less I trust the great powers in their diplomacy, in their understandings and in their secret undertakings. I fear Canada being drawn into a world conflict which is none of our doing.
In my opinion our British connection is our gravest danger. It is our gravest danger because we all-I am not an exception-worry about what would happen in London, what would happen in Glasgow or what would happen in all the other cities or counties which, because of our families, have come to mean a great deal to us. Yet I wonder whether, if we all-and there are only eleven millions of us, if there are that many; we could not say that there are twelve millions and not be exaggerating-went over and died for Europe, it would make the slightest difference.
There is a possibility, in spite of any assurance the minister may have made in the house, that when trouble breaks out in Europe, membership in a commonwealth, the heart of which although not exactly on the continent of Europe is uncomfortably near to it, will, because of public sentiment, carry us intb a conflict which, after all, has very little to do with North America-and I hope I can say the Americas.
So from that point of view I am becoming more and more north American in my outlook. It may be an escapist idea; that may be the reason I have worked it out, I do not know. I just know that increasingly I am thinking in terms of north America, and am determined that from my point of view we shall do what we can to save North America, because I am not sure that, with such a small population, we can do anything to save Europe. If she is determined to bring about her own destruction, that is not our business. Our business is to do what we can on the North American continent. If,

then, we are going to stress that fact, and if our national policy is going to be directed toward keeping out of European difficulties, and toward the protection of North America, I feel that more and more there should be understanding between the United States and Canada, because we share the Atlantic and Pacific coastlines. We are on the same continent; we think in the same continental terms, and, much as imperialists may deny it, Canada is becoming increasingly North American in her point of view. The young people growing up to-day are more and more aware that they are North Americans, and that the destiny of the Americas, or North America, is the thing which affects them most.
I do not say it will be impossible, but it will be more difficult than it was last time to inflame the youth of Canada to go again to fight in Europe. I think it can be done. With the radio, the press, an eloquent minister, and all the agencies which can be used when required, I think it can be done-and particularly when young men and women have little in life to interest them, when they have no economic security and when they have little chance of developing their capabilities. Here is a chance for adventure, even though it may mean death at the end. I think they can again be induced to leave our shores. I do not-and I am not speaking disrespectfully to the minister-believe that we can build up an efficient, mobile unit in Canada, and keep it in Canada, in the event of an outbreak of war in Europe. I am positive there is enough exchanging of staffs between Great Britain and Canada; I am positive there is enough imperialist sentiment in Canada to send our mobile force, or that part of it which can leave our shores, overseas; and that again, if war breaks out, it will be fought by us not here, but there.
I do not know that one can say more. I do not know whether one ought to strive to have the estimate cut down. I do not think we can defend our shores if this enemy which may come from either the west or the east is in dead earnest about it and has made up his mind to come in here. I cannot imagine a country the extent of Canada, with the small population we have, being defended by an expenditure of the estimate before the committee to-night. So that from the point of view of defence of the North American continent I think a great deal of it is wasted money. Frankly, I say to the minister I would rather open the schools in Saskatchewan. If we are going to do a lot towards killing everybody off, then let us do the best we can for them up to the last minute.

There may be something to be said for coastal defence. But I say just the same thing again-I cannot think of any other way to say it: If there were a great onslaught on either the west or the east coast, any defence we have would not count at all. In such a case we would have to depend upon someone else.
I do not think we are going to have an enemy invade Canada; I may be wrong, but I do not think so. I do not think they are even going to try to.
I hope not.

I do not think there is any grave danger. But if they do, we would simply have to rely upon someone else. It might be the British fleet upon which we would have to rely-but I have a very peculiar idea about that. I do not think the British fleet would be in our waters in such an event. They would be in other places where need for the fleet existed. I do not think they would be coming here. So do not depend upon that. I believe if there was an attack on Canada, the United States-and I dare say that is what the minister was referring to when he talked about " friendly fleets "-is the one place we could look to for assistance which would be given rapidly, not so much for our sake as for their own, because we happen to be their northern boundary. And so they would come, if they thought there was any grave danger to us.
I believe the discussion on the estimates will continue for another day or so; at least they will not be concluded to-night. After I have read what the minister said1-and after all, he read some of it-and have had an opportunity to read the translations of other speeches, I shall have a better idea of what people are thinking. But I have not changed my mind on what war is; it is just the same as before. There is no difference. The total disregard for human life, which we have suffered in Canada and which has been suffered all over the world since the last war, is the price we are still paying for the war we fought. If we have to face a further disregard for human life, it will be just that much worse. We shall not be any more successful after the next war. The concluding treaty will be no better than the treaty of Versailles. Like breeds like, and if we go on using the same methods of preparing for peace by getting ready for war, we shall get ready for war and get war-but not peace.

Recent events in the Sino-Japanese war, such as the bombing and sinking of the United States gunboat Panay, bring home to us the daily danger of an international conflict and emphasize the necessity of adequate protection for our shores.
With the present development of aerial combat, the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of Canada are in danger of attack in the event of either
England or the United States becoming involved in war. It is all very well to say that England and the United States will protect us. but we must have something with which to protect ourselves until they arrive.
The article is entitled " Lapointe's sane words."
For the sake of comparison, the Minister of Justice also took the city of Westmount, which, although it has a fire brigade of its own, nevertheless relies upon the whole Montreal fire brigade in the event of a conflagration. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), and other hon. ministers during by-elections, have had occasion to set forth quite clearly the present government's position as regards rearmament. Personally, only a few weeks after the estimates of National Defence were passed last year, I took part in the Bonaventure by-election. Later, for three weeks, it was my good fortune to join in the campaign carried on by the present member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Francceur), then government candidate in that constituency. Irrespective of any statements made in this regard, the question of national defence and armaments was discussed in Lotbiniere and in Bonaventure counties, as well as in the other counties-the question of armaments was for ever dinned into our ears wherever by-elections were held. During those campaigns, an attempt was made to have the electors of the province of Quebec believe that the government was prepared to enlist citizens of Canada to carry on hazardous enterprises abroad, which is positively untrue.
The people of Quebec province, especially those who urged us last year by their representations to oppose armaments, gave the reasons which, in their estimation, should justify us in voting against them. The main reason offered was this: Canada's participation in another war would increase the burden of taxation, overwhelming as it is already, and would lead the country into financial disaster, if not into absolute bankruptcy.
Another resolution was practically to the same effect. All of these representations did not so much oppose any increase of particular estimates as the possibility of the government joining perhaps in a race for armaments in preparation for a war outside of our territory.
We have heard these objections voiced by some of our friends here this afternoon, much to my regret. As far I am concerned, I stated last year that I felt the government could be trusted and I say it again. People outside politics, without any party affiliation, particularly with the Liberal party-and I will quote testimony to substantiate this-state in this
