Actual conditions, however, must be taken into account.
Our lack of knowledge in matters of national defence organization deters us from passing judgment on the amount of the appropriations sought by the government for the organization of the country's defence. We think it possible to place confidence in the government on that score, all the more so as the Prime Minister has emphasized the purely Canadian destination of this military expenditure.
These people, who are in no way bound to the Liberal party, find it possible to place confidence in the government on that score and add:
The Prime Minister has himself emphasized the purely Canadian destination of this military expenditure.
This afternoon the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) mentioned on several occasions the circumstances in which the right hon. the Prime Minister had publicly testified to his Canadianism for the greatest happiness of the country.
When people like that, in whom we have confidence and whose whole past is a guarantee that they will always place our country's interests before anything else, tell us that we should organize Canada's defence and that they have no other end in view, we should have confidence in them and support them as they were supported at the by-elections which have clearly expressed approval of the policy of the government on national defence.
Not being a great strategist and not wishing to give myself out as one before the house, I cannot say whether our defence, will cost 20, 40 or 50 million dollars. Neither am I ready to state, with all the equanimity shown by some of our friends, that Canada is in no danger of invasion and does not need to be protected. I am not disposed to take this attitude and, this year again, I intend to support the government and the ministers who have repeated, one after the other, that the appropriation asked for is solely for the protection of our homes against all possible danger from outside the country or against internal trouble.
Last year there was some discussion of dangers from inside the country. On March 30. 1937, speaking on the question of industrial disputes, repressive laws and communism, the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said:

This session we have taken means to increase another force we have available to maintain internal order in case of emergency, as well as to defend our coasts. I do not know whether it will astonish the house and the hon. member who has just spoken if I tell them that these increases in the estimates have been bitterly criticized by communists and those associated with communism in this country. I hold in my hand a circular which has been sent throughout Canada. One side is in English, the other side in French. It is the work of the association controlled by the communist party in Toronto, and is directed against those estimates.
It is strangesaid the minister of justice:
-that these people should be so strongly opposed to the provision I have mentioned.
Is it not your opinion? Here is an organization which is considered as extremely dangerous and undesirable, especially in the province of Quebec, an organization which we have the duty to fight and to annihilate in our country. When the government expresses the desire to provide the means of maintaining order in Canada, those who are opposed to communism are in league with the communists, unknowingly of course. But they cannot prevent a situation where the communists are associated with them when fighting against the organization for national defence and the maintenance of order in our country, a fact of great significance.
I will leave it at that. I just wanted to tell the government that, for my part, I am convinced that, in the circumstances, it is the duty of the government of the day to maintain in Canada, not a disproportionate army, but an adequate army for our needs. Such is the sentiment in my constituency and, I believe, in the province of Quebec.
I would have liked to quote the figures communicated to me last year by the deputy Minister of National Defence concerning our permanent force, but I do not have them here. However, it is a fact that the Canadian army, and more particularly the permanent force, is in need of reorganization and modernization. The government does not ask for anything beyond that. We have the assurance that the government of the day is not in favour of our participation in foreign wars. It is our duty to support them, to assure them that we appreciate their policy, and to tell them that, while voting increased appropriations for national defence we are irrevocably opposed to Canadian participation in any foreign conflict.
Mr. ARTHUR G. SLAGHT (Parry Sound): Mr. Chairman, in addressing the committee on this important subject I desire first to ally myself with the observations of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in the

Supply-National Defence
tribute that he paid to our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). Whether or not hon. members agree with the precise estimates which have been brought down, I think there can be but one opinion as to the fact that we in Canada to-day are singularly fortunate in having as our Minister of National Defence a man of the calibre of the gentleman who at present holds that important portfolio. He came to us from a race outstanding in British history, outstanding in the sacrifices that Scotland has made on the battlefields of the world; and those who believe in strict economy in measures of defence will have the added satisfaction that Scotchmen as a rule are not profligate with their dollars or the dollars entrusted to them to expend. So from the standpoint of the record of a race noted for its courage and its loyalty to the empire, and noted also for its economy where economy is desirable, we are indeed fortunate at this time in our nation's history in having at the helm of the national defence department the gentleman who occupies that position.
I support fully the estimates which he has submitted, and I propose to go a little farther than any hon. members who have so far addressed the committee, by making this rather humble suggestion that, in supplementary estimates perhaps, or in some other appropriate form, if not at this session then certainly at the next, a much more liberal expenditure be made by Canada in one of the branches of our defence services, namely in the service that comes under the heading of air force.	Last year we expended some
$10,000,000, and this year the estimates contemplate an expenditure of some $11,000,000 on this service. We have been given the details of the machines, the man power and the equipment of our present air service in Canada.
I was greatly impressed by some of the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) in the thoughtful contribution she made to this debate; they were sentiments which, in the main, inspire practically every hon. member. But may I suggest that, exercising the privilege which her sex have enjoyed for the last hundred years, she has changed her mind, in one respect; may I also suggest that, noble as those sentiments are, they failed to touch the exact point which is involved in the discussion of these estimates, and this I say with the greatest respect.
I desire to remind the committee, by citing a few figures, of what is the present armed state of the world. I believe that these figures are authentic, so far as it is possible to be accurate in matters of this kind; they
include not only standing armies ready for battle but reserves in the various countries referred to. Russia, with an enormous population, has an army of the type I have indicated of 15,000,000 men; France, an army of 6,000,000 men; Germany, with a population of 74,000,00, 2,900,000 men; Italy, with a population of 42,000,000, 2,450,000; Czechoslovakia, of which we have heard so much in recent days, approximately 1,250,000 men; Great Britain, 450,000 men. If I am correct, as I believe I am, our force in Canada consists of a permanent force of 4,000 men, and a paper force-and when I say that I shall be understood as meaning battalions which go to camp for perhaps two weeks in the year-

And not every year, as
my right hon. friend was kind enough to remind me-a force, I say, including reserves, of 75,000 men, and with a training force of 45,000. It is in support of what may properly be termed relatively a very meagre force that these estimates are presented, and they are absolutely necessary. Would any hon. member, bearing in mind the figures I have just quoted, suggest that in this day and age they should be reduced? Surely to put the question answers it.
I proceed to the particular branch of the estimates which attracts my special attention and as to which I have some remarks to make. I have already given the figures of expenditures on our air service in the past year and the expenditures proposed for the coming year. The minister told us that a year ago there were 1,080 men in our air force and that there is an estimated increase to 1.730, or an increase of 650 men. I have a suggestion to make which conforms, I understand, with a sentiment expressed this evening by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond), in a speech which, owing to my own lack of education, I regret I was unable to follow in the hon. member's native tongue. He referred to the viewpoint that the air force is a branch of the defence service which has an economic value in peace time, and it is in my view the only branch of our defence service which has an economic and constructive peace value. Soldiers on horseback, our infantry, and the branches of our service other than the air force have no economic peace time value. We are aware of the value of the air service because we are a party to the expenditures that are being made for the great transcontinental service which will come into effect next July. Those of us who follow air
Supply-National Defence

progress know that in the last year Canada carried by air five times as much freight as any other nation. That is a remarkable record.
Is that per capita?

Not per capita-gross. If I am correctly informed-and I believe I am- Canada carried five times as much freight in the air as any other nation, regardless of population. Therefore we should appreciate the strides which our country is making in this particular economic and military field, and the people of Canada and the members of this committee will be impressed by a viewpoint which has as its objective an increased expenditure on air service.
Let me remind the committee of one or two significent facts. I believe I am correct in saying that most of the machines in the military and perhaps also in the commercial branches of our air service are of low speed, and that the highest speed military machines we have, even including those under order, have no greater speed than 250 miles per hour.
Two hundred and eighty.
You had better not interpret them.
The hon. member was absent when I endeavoured to pay her a compliment for her contribution to the debate.
Thank you.

Who will say that it is impossible for this country to become involved in war? If we had a trained force of the type I have indicated, and if we were obliged to turn our minds at all to the problem of actual defence, how could we make a greater contribution to empire war service and empire
defence-including our own selfish defenoe- than to have a force of 1,000 trained airmen equipped with a large number of machines of high-powered type, together with other machines of lower velocity and a mechanical force of 7,000 men to service that fleet of planes? Could we hope by any other means to make so great a contribution to ultimate world peace, which I assume is the desire of every hon. member.
I commend this suggestion to the minister. It must not be forgotten that such a force would have a definite economic peace time value. I believe that the development of air traffic, both passenger and freight, is in its infancy; and just as twenty-five years ago the first hard-tired small automobiles came upon the scene, so for the next generation progress in transportation will be in the air-transportation for economic and, I regret to say, destructive purposes. With a population of eleven million we cannot compete with the armies I have outlined; we could not begin to compete with them; it would be stupidity on our part to attempt to do so. But here is a branch of service that would be eminently useful-and I speak from the records of the last great war. By common consent, even on the part of Britain's enemies in that war, Canadian pilots and mechanics outshone the pilots and mechanics of every other nation. That is a well established fact.
I desire, with some diffidence, to present for the earnest consideration of the committee the observations I have just made as to a field in which we may engage. Do not let us wait until the nations of the world are at war before we prepare.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), who has just taken his seat, had continued a little further with his discussion of the air service, perhaps I should not have arisen. As he proceeded with his remarks I thought, in connection with the aeroplanes to which he was referring, for bombing and so on, he would have coupled with that subject some remarks in reference to rescue work as a result of gas bombs being dropped from the air, and if that had been done perhaps I should not have said anything at this time.
I thank my hon. friend for that reminder. It is a real factor, and I overlooked it.

I remember sitting in the Friedrichstrasse station in Berlin, Germany, for a matter of three hours last June, after I had finished my investigation into various matters in that city. I became attracted by
Supply-National Defence

the- large number of aviators who were entering and leaving that station. First, I was interested in the bands on their arms, which all seemed to be different; then I commenced counting the number who got on and off each train. According to my memory a train entered or left the station about every four minutes; there were many tracks. I was putting in my time and commenced figuring an average of how many got on and off. Finally, I computed that the average number of aviators per train getting on or off was twenty. At the rate of fifteen trains an hour that meant three hundred aviators an hour, and for the three hours I sat there it meant nine hundred aviators.
I must confess that I left Berlin that night feeling greatly depressed, thinking that if the British Empire should become involved in any trouble with Germany, that country would have a very large number of trained aviators. I inquired how many they had, and was told that they numbered something between eight and ten thousand aviators ready to take the air at any time. Throughout the city itself I found preparations being carried on to protect its inhabitants, who number some four or five million, by means of shelters where the people could go in the event of the city being gassed.
The point I am making is that whether or not we like trouble, it comes to us, and to every nation, and at this moment I might add that I certainly approve the minister doing the best he can. I have no comment to make at the moment on the estimates except the omission, as I see it, of a vote to provide some defence against attack by gas in this country. However, a moment ago I started to say that throughout the city of Berlin they were preparing or planning places of refuge. When I returned to England I found similar plans there, and on going to the Home Office I learned that adequate preparation is being carried on in that country. I do not know of any preparations along this line being carried on in Canada. The minister may have in mind some protection against the effects of air raids on the civilian population in regard to gas, but I do not see anything in the estimates for it.
That is being very carefully considered at the present moment.

I am glad to learn that. I should like to take just a few moments to tell the committee the preparations that are being carried on in the old country. As I said, I went to the Home Office and found

that they had divided England into eleven districts; I do not know about Scotland and Ireland. These districts were as follows: London, Salisbury. Cardiff, Birmingham, Shrewsbury, Liverpool, Newcastle, Leeds, York, Nottingham and Cambridge. All these districts were again subdivided to take care of the counties and municipalities adjacent thereto. Hearing that a great demonstration was to take place in the city of Leeds, I went there to learn what I could. Perhaps the minister was there also. The evening I was there I attended a school held for the purpose of educating the people in how to protect themselves against gas. There is no use in fooling ourselves or, to use a common expression, in kidding ourselves that we are safe in Canada. To-day no country is safe, and it is only fit and proper that every country should make preparations to protect its civilians.
What did I find in Leeds, at that school? I found a gentleman, I suppose an officer from the Home Office, and I might add that the school was held in a large auditorium in the city hall, which was packed with people who were in deadly earnest, listening to what the officer from London told them. He said that an air raid might take place without anyone being notified about it; that the Home Office, through the air marshal, would try to advise the sub-air marshals in the various districts that an air raid was impending, and this officer did his best to tell the people there assembled how they might protect themselves. I believe this can be done here, outside any possibility of Canada taking part in a war. I do not believe any hon. member wants to see Canada engaged in a war; I think every hon. member wants Canada to keep out of war, but whether we like it or not, it may come our way, and we might come right up against what this officer told the people that night in Leeds. I attended a school in another city as well, but I shall confine my remarks to what I learned that night at Leeds.
What did the officer ask them? He asked the people there assembled to volunteer-to do what? To divide themselves into various classes; to make preparation for what might come like a thief in the night, namely, a gas attack, without warning. The first class was the first aid and medical service class. He invited doctors, nurses, people belonging to the St. John's Ambulance Corps and other similar associations to join that class and volunteer to give assistance in Leeds in the event of an air raid. They were to be ready to go to the aid of casualties; to give them conveyance by ambulance to hospitals, and to keep the citizens instructed as to how to put on their

Supply-National Defence
gas masks. Just in passing I might say that before I left Berlin I made inquiry as to how many gas masks the German government had available, and I was told about forty-five million. In England I learned that they had about thirty-five million gas masks. When the minister speaks on this matter again, I should like him to tell us something of the preparations which are being made in Canada in connection with the provision for gas masks.
WThen the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) was speaking this afternoon, I wondered what would happen if one of these great aeroplane carriers sailed into Hudson bay. The planes would have to go only a few hundred miles to reach Cochrane, and I doubt if there is a gas mask in that town. If Cochrane were showered with gas they would all be in danger; there would be no possibility of saving their lives. It would be the same thing in Toronto; I do not know that there are any gas masks in that city. Would the minister tell us what preparation is being made in Canada, so far as gas masks are concerned, and particularly for the protection of our coastal cities, both east and west, such as Halifax, St. John and Vancouver? If there is no expenditure indicated in the estimates to cover that point, I am one who believes that there should be some provision for gas masks to save the people who might live in cities or towns bombed from the air by gas.
The second division they were instructed to prepare for was in connection with rescue parties and the demolition of buildings. We see pictures in illustrated papers of buildings which have been bombed, showing what is taking place in Spain. Squads must be in readiness to tear down damaged buildings, because a wall leaning over as a result of a bomb presents a danger. Volunteers are called to do that kind of work. There must also be men to clear the roads, or to repair steam pipes which have been opened by an explosion. I do not know whether we are doing anything along this line in Canada.
We may be on the verge of attack-I hope we are not; I hope we are never attacked. But it would not do us any harm to be ready to take care of ourselves if we were attacked from the air or otherwise. The officer next called for volunteers to attend to the decontamination of buildings and roadways, as a result of a town or city being gassed from the air. This particular service calls for the cleaning up of roads and the sprinkling of lime on them, or some other decontaminator, which would destroy the effects of gas.
The officer next asked for air raid wardens. These are volunteers who would be ready to fly at a moment's notice to warn people by means of sirens that the city was about to be gassed. He also asked that volunteers, to wear the necessary protective appliances, be enrolled to go here and there throughout the city, to various sections and places, to detect places filled with gas. He gave long instructions with respect to the preparation of rooms.
I wonder if we have anything like that in Canada. I brought back the literature which was handed to me-all sorts of it. Pamphlet No 1, is entitled, Organization of Air Raid Casualty Services. Have we anything of that kind sent out in Canada? If we have not, then we should have. No. 2 is entitled. Rescue Parties and Clearance of Debris. We should have some organization ready, in the event of a city like Halifax being bombed from an aircraft carrier. Who can tell that Halifax could be saved by any surface craft if an aircraft carrier, coming within range of the city, sent out bombing planes and showered it with gas? How would the people know what to do? Has the department sent out literature? If the department has not literature along the lines of that published in England, it should have.
Pamphlet No 3, is entitled, Organization of Decontamination Services, and No 4, is Air Raid Wardens. I had not intended saying anything, but I was moved to do so by the observations of the hon. member for Parry Sound. All I can say to the minister is that if there is no service available at the present time, or no money provided through an estimate for the protection of Canadians against air raids, against bombing and gas attacks from the air, then any vote along that line should be supported by the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but certain statements were made which prompt me to make_ a few observations. Last year, when we discussed the question of armaments, I stood by the government. We were somewhat criticized in our constituencies, but I was glad to notice, this year, a change of opinion among the public, and even among some members of this house. I am sure that many of those who criticized us last year will have to admit now that we were right then as we are to-day in supporting the government.
War is a terrible thing. We are all agreed on that, and nobody wants war, neither those who are in favour of armaments nor the others,
Supply-National Defence

but, as the hon. member who just spoke said, war will break out when we least expect it, and without notice.
There is in the province of Quebec a most vulnerable spot, in case of war. I mean the St. Maurice valley. I want the people who inhabit this valley to hear what might happen if a war broke out. With the powerful aircraft that are in use to-day, we know that our enemies would attempt to attack mainly the spots where our war industries are situated. Tor instance, in the St. Maurice valley there are cities like Three Rivers, Shawinigan and Grand'Mere where many industries are apt to manufacture war materials. At the head of the St. Maurice valley there is the Gouin dam which w*as built, I believe, some twenty-five years ago, and which forms a reservoir containing so much water that, if it were bombed, it would flood the whole St. Maurice valley. It could possibly drown the whole population and completely destroy our war industries.
I do not wish to censure any of my colleagues, but I just want to ask those who are residing in the St. Maurice valley to ponder over this contingency. Supposing an airplane would get to that dam at a speed of 400 miles an hour, and destroy it with bombs, would it not be a terrible disaster? The hon. members from that district have every good reason to see Canada well armed.
Nobody likes war, either on this side or on the other side of this house, and we have finally agreed on the question of armaments. I notice also that hon. members of the opposition who, last year, remained silent during the discussion of these estimates, now come forward and are more ready than ever to support the government.

Mr. Chairman. I listened with a great deal of interest this afternoon to the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). I say I listened with interest, because one does become interested when expressions are given by ministers of the crown on such matters as national defence, and matters touching upon problems of the day and their relation to other nations. I do not think the minister could have said anything but what he did. If any of us were in the same position we could not have said anything more. I am not now speaking for the group to which I belong. My personal observation is that if we were to find ourselves on the treasury benches we would not know just what to do in connection with foreign policy. We have often been asked just what we would do in connection with finance, and although the 
answer has not always been to the satisfaction of hon. members opposite, I think we would know just what should be done. But when it comes to the problems being debated to-night, I doubt if we would know just how to act. In saying that, I do not think I admit any weakness on our part; it simply illustrates that the problems which confront the government of this and other countries are so exacting that it would be difficult indeed to determine the proper and exact course to follow.
I am in accord with some of the things said by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail). I cannot see any sense in spending money on armaments and then permitting war materials to go from this country to potential enemies. I imagine all hon. members will agree with that. However, there are other matters to be considered. We all like to be idealistic to a certain extent; we all know in our own minds what we would like to see done; but we cannot very well deal with things as we would like them to be; we must deal with them as they are. Things being as they are in the world to-day, who can say just what should be done?
I experience a little difficulty in knowing just where the work of the Minister of National Defence ends and the work of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his capacity as Secretary of State for External Affairs, begins. I have never been able to determine the exact line of demarcation. When we are debating or discussing matters pertaining to estimates on national defence, we are so likely to slide off into matters of foreign policy. In some instances we feel that we have to do this. However, I think we should appreciate the position in which the Prime Minister finds himself these days. Sometimes I have felt that he has not given an adequate and full answer to some questions concerning foreign policy; yet at the same time I do not think we should try to embarrass the government.
I do not believe there is a man living who can predict what will happen in the next few months or even in the next few weeks. I do not think it is wise for us to ask the Prime Minister for a specific and definite answer with regard to foreign policy because he may have to change that answer in a few months. I am reminded of a book written by Sir Norman Angell. I shall not quote from that book as some hon. members do not appreciate quotations. Prior to the great war he wrote a book entitled The Great Illusion, in which he dealt with the money aspect of a possible war. It has since been

Supply-National Defence
proven that when that war did break out, every one of his contentions were erroneous. His predictions did not come true. Sir Norman Angell is nobody's fool; he is a smart man in many ways; but he could not make accurate predictions at that time, and conditions to-day are tremendously more problematical than they were then. I am not saying that we are nearer to war, but it seems to me that the world's stage as it appears to-day is more intricate than it was then. If such men as he were unable to say with any degree of certainty what would happen in the future, who can do so to-day? I would be reluctant to embarrass the government in this connection.
There are one or two observations I should like to make with regard to the closing part of the minister's speech. These observations may seem trivial, but I should like to place them before the committee. The minister said that we were a free people, but I do not think we are. We may be free to vote and elect a government, but I doubt very much if that government is free once it is in office. We are not free, even as a nation, to do as we would like to do. Our contention is that the present system of finance will not permit it.
If I understood the minister correctly, he said that to a large extent governments were guided by popular opinion. He had better think over that statement a little more as I doubt whether it is so in fact. If he will reflect a little more, he must realize that certain factors go toward moulding public opinion and those factors are often brought into play by the action of governments. There are many illustrations of this in history. For instance, take the ease of the abdication of Edward. In that instance the popular cry was that he should remain, come what may. But Mr. Stanley Baldwin thought otherwise and paid little heed to the cry of public opinion.
We all recognize, I think, that statesmen must be very far-seeing. Sometimes public opinion is not right, and again, public opinion changes very, very rapidly. I would not advise our government to be swayed by public opinion, because public opinion to-day may be one thing and to-morrow it may be entirely different, and sometimes it does not take very much to change it. I suppose that public opinion with regard to conscription, for the sake of illustration, would be opposed to it; but if an incident such as that of the sinking of the Lusitania occurred, or if the newspapers were to print war atrocities and display cartoons showing babies stuck on the end of bayonets, public opinion would change very, very rapidly.
I have made these observations, Mr. Chairman, as my small contribution to this debate, and it may not be worth very much. I feel, of course, that money policy plays a big part in all these things, and this group goes a step farther in saying that until the money system is so adjusted as to bring about a conformity between money and the distribution of goods and services, there will in the end be no peace. Money knows no international boundaries, and until this adjustment is brought about, there will be no peace.

I should like to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, before this item carries. First, I should like to quote a remark made by the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he was dealing with defence estimates in 1937, as reported at page 1040 of Hansard of that year. He said:
I should be inclined to believe that the security of one's country would rank as the first among all social securities.
That, of course, is a statement with which no one can quarrel, and it is as true to-day as it was then. Dealing with the principle which has been laid down by imperial conferences since time immemorial, and which was referred to by the minister in his remarks to-day, he said:
The primary responsibility of each portion of the empire is for its own local defence.
In dealing with the local defence of a country such as Canada, I would point out that the vital areas extend for some very considerable distance beyond our harbours on the east coast and on the west as well. Local defence, using the term in its narrowest sense, if it is to be adequate must include such sea-going craft as can cope effectively with enemy warships, and in particular with enemy craft of the type known as the cruiser raider, such as the Emden, which wrought so much havoc during the past war.
Dealing with the phrase " local defence " and with our naval situation in particular, I would submit that as we are now equipped on the sea, or as we shall be even after the present estimates have been appropriated and spent, we shall have nothing that could be described as adequate for the defence of Halifax, Saint John, Vancouver and Victoria. The failure to make provision for purchasing a cruiser is, I contend, a glaring gap in the estimates as they stand, and our destroyer fleet would be entirely ineffective in coping with the type of raid that the Emden carried on during the last war, and with the type of raid that we may expect with full confidence will be suffered by our ports, not some weeks after war breaks out, but within a very few

Supply-National Defence
hours after the declaration of war. I would also remind the minister that declarations of war have gone out of fashion. What I am trying to emphasize is the extreme urgency of adequate protection on the sea, which is lacking at the present time.
We should also have, in my opinion, submarines in order that the focal waters around Saint John, Halifax, Vancouver and Victoria may be protected. Before I leave the eastern ports I should like to touch on their tremendous importance in any scheme of empire defence. Military experts agree that within the United Kingdom at the present time there is enough food to last approximately six weeks and no more. In the event of a war which included the United Kingdom there are two possibilities: The United States might participate in the early stages of the war, and the United States might not. In this house in our deliberations we should prepare for either eventuality.
Let us take the second one, a war in which the United States takes no part. The situation then would be that the United States, by their neutrality legislation, would be prohibited from shipping anything to the belligerents. No food, no munitions, no nickel, no copper could leave the United States for the British Isles if the United States were not involved in the war. That would place a tremendous burden on the ports of Saint John and Halifax. It would make those ports of primary importance in any scheme of imperial defence, and as they are now protected, my submission is that these ports would be put out of action within the first week of the war. They are absolutely vulnerable to attack by the cruiser-raider type of vessel. Furthermore, there is an entire lack, so far as I know, and so far as these estimates or the minister's statements have revealed, of any adequate, modern antiaircraft equipment. The ports are at the mercy of attacks not only from the sea but from such planes as would inevitably slip through any North sea blockade that might be established, some carried by aircraft carriers and some in the holds of merchantmen, which would establish themselves somewhere within 250 miles of Saint John and Halifax, up north, Labrador way, where it would be practically impossible to locate them until great damage had been done. Using their ships as their base, they would run a shuttle bombing service which in a very short time would put the ports of Saint John and Halifax entirely out of action. The result of that would be that not only food, for which Great Britain would be looking to this country, but the all important supplies of nickel, copper

and other sinews of war, which would have to come from the North American continent, would be entirely lacking.
The minister in his statement said that the use of modern aircraft had turned the probability of attacks from the air into a possibility.
The very opposite-the possibility into a probability.

I stand corrected-yes.	I
would go one step further, and say that it has become an absolute certainty in the event of war. I point out another probability, if not a certainty, namely, that cities such as Quebec -certainly-and	Montreal-possibly-would
be subject to bombing attacks by dirigibles which would come in by way of Labrador, which would be seen by nobody except a few Indians, and which would be in a position to unload, without any warning whatever, two tons of explosives on the city of Quebec.
The same possibility, probability, or certainty exists in so far as the cities of Vancouver and Victoria are concerned. It is true that at the present time we have the British navy; we have had it for years, and we rely with a sense of security upon what that navy can do for us. But the fact of the matter is that if a war of world dimensions broke out-and personally I fail to see how any modern war can be other than one of world dimensions-the British navy would have all it could possibly do to protect the focal waters around the British Isles. There would be no possibility of the navy sending detachments to protect this part of the empire. Furthermore, we have no right to expect that that would be done, because, as imperial conference after imperial conference has affirmed, as the Prime Minister himself stated in his speech of February a year ago, and as the minister reiterated to-night, the primary responsibility of each portion of the empire is for its own local defence.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I protest against the entire lack of adequate provision in these estimates for the protection of those very parts of the country which the Prime Minister over a year ago referred to as vulnerable points, points which must be protected. I quote further from the remarks of the Prime Minister. At page 1041 of Hansard he said:
With warfare what it is likely to be in the future, with possible air and submarine raids and all else that is to be feared, the protection of our great municipalities against the dropping of bombs or the sowing of mines which might disrupt the whole life of a municipality, becomes one of the most serious obligations under the heading of present day defence.

We have been sitting in this chamber now for two months, and have devoted much time to the discussion of all sorts of resolutions, many of them of very little moment. We have talked at endless length about the advisability of designing and adopting a new Canadian flag which will signify our status as an "equality partner in the empire."
